stem: A 74-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of vague upper abdominal pain associated with progressive yellowish discoloration of his skin and sclera and dark urine. On examination, he was jaundiced (see lab result and report). Test Result Normal Values Alkaline phosphatase 312 39-117 IU/L Direct bilirubin 87 1.5-6.5 mol/L Total bilirubin 97 3.5-16.5 mol/L Ultrasound: Dilated intrahepatic biliary tree with collapsed gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Progressive obstructive jaundice (dark urine, high ALP and direct bilirubin) in a 74-year-old with US showing dilated intrahepatic biliary tree and a collapsed gallbladder puts the block at the hepatic duct confluence, above the cystic duct. Bile cannot reach the gallbladder, so it stays empty: this is a Klatskin tumour (hilar cholangiocarcinoma).
why_wrong_block:
B. Mirizzi's syndrome: due to a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, so the gallbladder contains stones and is inflamed with RUQ pain; right in a gallstone patient with CHD compression.
C. Gallbladder cancer: shows a gallbladder mass or wall thickening, often with gallstones, rather than a simply collapsed empty gallbladder.
D. Periampullary tumour: a distal block dilates both intra- and extrahepatic ducts and distends the gallbladder (Courvoisier).
key_concept:
Collapsed gallbladder + intrahepatic dilatation only = obstruction above the cystic duct.
  • Klatskin: hilar, collapsed gallbladder
  • Periampullary / pancreatic head: distal, distended gallbladder, both duct systems dilated
  • Mirizzi: stone in gallbladder neck compressing CHD
exam_pearl: Do not choose periampullary just because the patient is old with jaundice; the collapsed gallbladder is the decisive clue.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the source.

stem: The vascular surgeon was called for help in the Operating Room by the colorectal surgeon who is doing a low anterior resection for colon cancer as he encountered pelvic bleeding that he could not control. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Uncontrollable pelvic bleeding during a low anterior resection is classically from the presacral venous plexus or pelvic vessels in a deep, narrow field. The first move is heavy packing of the pelvis with direct pressure, which tamponades venous bleeding, buys time for the anaesthetist to resuscitate, and lets the team regroup before any further step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Do on table angiogram: takes time and needs a stable patient; angiography and embolisation are for persistent arterial bleeding after temporary control.
C. Infra renal aortic clamp: does not control venous plexus bleeding and is not the first step; aortic clamping is reserved for failure of packing with ongoing haemorrhage.
D. Supra celiac aortic clamp: a rescue step when the patient becomes profoundly hypotensive despite packing (the follow-up scenario), not the initial manoeuvre.
key_concept:
Ladder for uncontrolled intraoperative pelvic bleeding.
  • Step 1: pack the pelvis with pressure and resuscitate
  • Packing fails with profound hypotension: supraceliac aortic clamp
  • Then definitive control once resuscitated (repair, ligation, embolisation, or damage control)
exam_pearl: Pressure and packing first; clamps and angiography come only when packing fails.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: The vascular surgeon was called for help in the Operating Room by the colorectal surgeon who is doing a low anterior resection for colon cancer as he encountered pelvic bleeding that he could not control, the pelvis was packed and the bleeding slowed down but the patient dropped his pressure again. Blood pressure 60/40 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptD: Remove the packs and repair the injury
why_right: The pelvis has already been packed, yet the patient has dropped his pressure again to 60/40, meaning ongoing life-threatening haemorrhage. The key here is a supraceliac aortic clamp: it can be applied quickly at the diaphragmatic hiatus away from the bloody pelvic field, controls all aortic inflow and maintains perfusion to the heart and brain while resuscitation catches up and definitive control is planned.
why_wrong_block:
A. Do on table angiogram: too slow for a patient at 60/40; angiography and embolisation suit a patient stable enough to wait.
B. Infra renal aortic clamp: needs dissection close to the retroperitoneal and pelvic haematoma and gives less proximal control; it is used for elective aortic work or bleeding with time to expose the infrarenal aorta.
D. Remove the packs and repair the injury: removing packs in a hypotensive patient restarts uncontrolled bleeding; repair comes after inflow control and resuscitation.
key_concept:
Pelvic bleeding during LAR, stepwise.
  • First: heavy pelvic packing
  • Packing in place but BP crashes (60/40): supraceliac aortic clamp
  • Then resuscitate and achieve definitive control
exam_pearl: Note the twist from the first version of this case: packing done and still hypotensive switches the answer from packing to supraceliac clamping.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot; 'Infra' and 'Supra' highlighted in red for contrast.

stem: A 37-year-old complained of a right breast lump for 3 months. She has family history of breast cancer. Physical examination confirmed a hard lump in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast with ill-defined edge and skin tethering and no palpable axillary lymph node. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A 37-year-old with a family history and a hard, ill-defined lump with skin tethering needs triple assessment, and in a woman older than 30 the next step is imaging: bilateral mammography (with or without ultrasound). Imaging comes before biopsy so the lesion is characterised and the other breast is screened, and the biopsy then targets the lesion without distorting the images.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI breast: a problem-solving or high-risk screening tool (e.g. known BRCA, dense breasts, occult primary), not the first test for a palpable lump.
B. Core needle biopsy: the definitive tissue diagnosis and the step after imaging; it becomes the answer once mammography or US shows a suspicious (BI-RADS 4 or 5) lesion.
D. Fine needle aspiration cytology: gives cytology only, cannot distinguish invasive from in situ disease or give receptor status; core biopsy has replaced it for solid lumps.
key_concept:
Breast lump workup = triple assessment: exam, imaging, biopsy.
  • Age under 30: ultrasound first
  • Age 30 or more: mammography with or without ultrasound
  • Suspicious imaging (BI-RADS 4/5): core needle biopsy
  • MRI: selected high-risk or problem-solving cases
exam_pearl: Malignant-sounding features tempt you to jump to biopsy, but the first step at 30 or older is still mammography.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: ** marks C (Bilateral mammography); B (Core needle biopsy) is separately highlighted in blue in the screenshot.
Other marked answers: Blue highlight in screenshot: B. Core needle biopsy

stem: A 33-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle crash. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious and alert. Examination showed an open wound to the anterior surface of the neck with devitalized tissue. Blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, Heart rate 104 /min, Respiratory rate 28 /min, Oxygen saturation 87%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: open wound to the anterior surface of the neck
why_right: Airway comes first. This patient has an open anterior neck wound with devitalized tissue, is tachypnoeic (RR 28) and hypoxic at SpO2 87%; saturation below 88% is an indication for a definitive airway. While he is still conscious, endotracheal intubation secures the airway before swelling or haematoma make it impossible.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxygen mask: adequate for a hypoxic trauma patient with a protected airway, but here the airway is threatened by the neck wound and saturation is already below 88%.
B. Tracheostomy: a formal, slower surgical airway for elective or semi-elective settings, not the emergency step.
C. Cricothyroidotomy: the emergency surgical airway when intubation fails or is impossible (severe maxillofacial trauma, cannot intubate cannot oxygenate).
key_concept:
Trauma indications for a definitive airway (intubation).
  • SpO2 below 88% despite oxygen
  • GCS 8 or less / unconscious
  • Risk of aspiration (oral bleeding, secretions)
  • Threatened airway: neck wound, expanding haematoma, burns
  • Intubation fails or impossible: cricothyroidotomy
exam_pearl: Conscious and alert does not mean a safe airway; hypoxia plus a neck wound means intubate now.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: ** marks D (Endotracheal intubation); A (Oxygen mask) carries a separate darker highlight in the screenshot.
Other marked answers: Highlight in screenshot: A. Oxygen mask

stem: A 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department after he was involved in motor vehicle crash, which was driving at a speed of 130 km/hour. Patient was wearing seat belt. On arrival to the Emergency Department, he was conscious, and alert (see report). Chest X-ray: Normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: High-speed blunt trauma (130 km/h) warrants abdominal imaging, and this patient is conscious and alert, i.e. treated as haemodynamically stable, with a normal chest X-ray. The stable blunt abdominal trauma patient goes for CT abdomen (with contrast), which grades solid organ injury and detects hollow viscus and retroperitoneal injury.
why_wrong_block:
A. US abdomen (FAST): the bedside test for the unstable patient to look for free fluid; it misses many solid organ, bowel and retroperitoneal injuries.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy: used mainly for suspected diaphragmatic injury or equivocal penetrating trauma in a stable patient, not as first evaluation.
D. Exploratory laparotomy: for unstable patients with positive FAST, peritonitis, evisceration or gunshot wounds, none of which is present.
key_concept:
Abdominal trauma triage by stability.
  • Stable: CT abdomen
  • Unstable blunt: FAST; positive leads to laparotomy
  • Peritonitis, evisceration or unstable with free fluid: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Stability decides the test: stable goes to CT, unstable gets FAST.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: IUGR neonate placed under warmer, he is still hypothermic despite warm environment, how to manage
OptC: Reassure + change environment ( increase warmer temperature i guess)
why_right: Temperature instability, especially hypothermia that persists despite a warm environment, is a classic sign of neonatal sepsis. Once environmental cause is excluded (he is already under a warmer), the neonate needs a sepsis workup (blood culture, CBC, CRP, consider LP) and prompt empirical IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. Checking and correcting glucose is part of care in an IUGR neonate, but IV dextrose treats hypoglycemia, not the cause of refractory hypothermia; it is right when the glucose is documented low.
C. Simply turning up the warmer and reassuring ignores the warning sign; adjusting the environment is right only when the baby is cold because of an inadequate thermal environment.
D. Skin-to-skin contact is a good first measure for routine thermal care of a stable newborn, but it does not address hypothermia that persists despite active warming.
key_concept:
Persistent neonatal hypothermia despite adequate warming = suspect sepsis until proven otherwise.
  • Neonatal sepsis signs are nonspecific: temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, apnea, hypoglycemia
  • Neonates (especially preterm/IUGR) often get hypothermia rather than fever with infection
  • Workup: blood culture, CBC, CRP, consider LP
  • Start empirical IV antibiotics without waiting for results
exam_pearl: First fix the environment; if the baby stays cold despite a warmer, the problem is the baby, so think sepsis.

stem: 10 years old sudden loss of consciousness then regained while running. all physical examination normal except ejection systolic murmur. What Is the most appropriate test?
why_right: Syncope during exertion (while running) plus an ejection systolic murmur is a red flag for left ventricular outflow obstruction, mainly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis. Echocardiography directly shows the structure (septal thickness, valve, outflow gradient), so it is the most appropriate test to establish the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. ECG is a reasonable screening test and helps for arrhythmic causes (long QT, WPW), but it cannot define a structural lesion behind a murmur; it would be the key if the scenario pointed to an arrhythmia, for example palpitations with a normal exam.
C. Chest X-ray is nonspecific for heart size and lungs and cannot diagnose HCM or valve stenosis.
D. Reassurance fits a typical vasovagal faint at rest with an innocent murmur; exertional syncope with a murmur is never innocent.
key_concept:
Exertional syncope + systolic murmur = structural heart disease until proven otherwise; echo.
  • HCM: murmur louder with Valsalva or standing
  • Aortic stenosis: ejection murmur radiating to the carotids
  • Innocent murmur: asymptomatic, soft, systolic, changes with position
  • Arrhythmic causes (long QT, WPW): ECG
exam_pearl: Syncope at rest with prodrome is vasovagal; syncope DURING exercise is cardiac until proven otherwise.

stem: 9 year old girl suspected of appendicitis(they stated that), complain of right lower quadrant pain, no fever no anorexia and no rebound tenderness WBC 9 What is the best thing to do to avoid missing the diagnosis?
OptA: Admit and do serial examination and repeat lap in 6-12 hrs
OptC: Discharge patient with given instructions when to come back
highlight_terms_source: no fever no anorexia and no rebound tenderness
why_right: This 9-year-old has RLQ pain only, with no fever, no anorexia, no rebound and a normal WBC of 9: a low-probability picture for appendicitis. The safest way to avoid missing an evolving appendicitis is active observation: admit, repeat the abdominal examination and repeat the labs over 6 to 12 hours, so that the signs declare themselves without exposing the child to unnecessary radiation or surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT: avoided in children because of radiation; when imaging is needed in a child, ultrasound is first line, and CT is kept for equivocal cases or complications such as abscess.
C. Discharge patient with given instructions: reasonable only for a very low-risk patient with reliable follow-up, but the question asks how to avoid missing the diagnosis, which needs in-hospital serial assessment.
key_concept:
Suspected appendicitis: act on the probability.
  • Low probability (no fever, no rebound, normal WBC): admit, serial exam and repeat labs
  • Equivocal, child or pregnant: ultrasound first
  • Equivocal adult or obese adult: CT
  • High probability (classic picture, rebound, leukocytosis): appendectomy
exam_pearl: Normal WBC and no peritonism do not exclude early appendicitis; serial examination is the safety net.

stem: A child presented with low grade fever for 2 days then developed of acute onset of stridor What is the most common cause?
why_right: A low grade fever for 2 days (viral prodrome) followed by stridor is the typical course of croup (viral laryngotracheitis or laryngotracheobronchitis), most often due to parainfluenza virus. It is by far the most common cause of acute stridor in children.
why_wrong_block:
A. Epiglottitis is now rare and presents abruptly with high fever, a toxic look, drooling and tripod position, not a mild low grade prodrome.
B. Acute tonsillitis causes sore throat, fever and dysphagia but does not usually cause stridor unless complicated by a large abscess.
key_concept:
Viral prodrome + barking cough + inspiratory stridor in a well looking child = croup.
  • Cause: parainfluenza virus
  • Clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed
  • Treatment: steroids; nebulized epinephrine if distress
  • Toxic, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, secure the airway
  • Toxic and not responding to croup treatment: bacterial tracheitis
  • Sudden choking, no prodrome: foreign body
exam_pearl: Low grade fever and a well child point to croup; high fever, drooling and a toxic look flip it to epiglottitis.

stem: A 3-year-old child with bronchial asthma on ventolin nebulizer at home as per needs. The mother expresses concern that the family cannot go out of the home most of the time because the nebulizer machine need electricity power source. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling should be given?
OptA: Agree and support their decision as the priority is asthma control
OptB: Find someone to take care of asthmatic child if family goes out of the home
OptC: Educate with clear instructions inhaler usage and advice to stop nebulizer
OptD: Find out nebulizer machine with portability feature
highlight_terms_source: cannot go out of the home
why_right: Salbutamol given by metered dose inhaler with a spacer (plus face mask at age 3) is as effective as a nebulizer and is portable. Since the nebulizer needing electricity is restricting family life, the right counselling is to teach correct inhaler and spacer technique and stop the nebulizer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Accepting a confined lifestyle is unnecessary because equal asthma control is possible with a portable inhaler and spacer.
B. Arranging a caregiver does not fix the real problem (the device) and isolates the child from family life.
D. A portable nebulizer adds cost and still is not needed, since an inhaler with spacer is equally effective and already portable.
key_concept:
Children: MDI + spacer (with face mask if young) = nebulizer in effectiveness, and more practical.
  • Young child: MDI + spacer + face mask
  • Older child: MDI + spacer with mouthpiece
  • Poor control: check technique and adherence first
  • Frequent symptoms on SABA alone: add inhaled steroid
exam_pearl: Counselling questions reward the option that fixes the cause with equal efficacy, not the one that accommodates the problem.

stem: Picture of pediatric feet nails with koilonychia, the child presented with pallor, lethargy, and fatigue, CBC shows microcytic hypo-chromic RBC, What is the treatment ?
why_right: Koilonychia (spoon nails) with pallor, lethargy and fatigue and a microcytic hypochromic CBC is iron deficiency anemia. The lead in asks for treatment, and the first line treatment of IDA in a child who can take tablets or syrup is oral ferrous sulfate. Response is checked by a rise in reticulocytes and hemoglobin after starting oral iron.
why_wrong_block:
A. Parenteral iron is reserved for failure of oral iron: malabsorption (e.g. celiac or IBD), true intolerance or persistent nonadherence. Nothing here suggests oral therapy has failed.
C. Folic acid deficiency gives a megaloblastic macrocytic anemia; this smear is microcytic and hypochromic.
D. B12 deficiency is also macrocytic and may bring neurological signs; it does not cause spoon nails or a microcytic picture.
key_concept:
Microcytic hypochromic anemia plus koilonychia = iron deficiency; treat with oral ferrous sulfate first.
  • IDA signs: pallor, fatigue, pica, koilonychia, angular cheilitis, glossitis
  • IDA labs: low ferritin, MCV, MCH; high TIBC, RDW, platelets
  • High RDW favors IDA; normal RDW favors thalassemia trait
  • No response to adequate oral iron: think thalassemia, so do Hb electrophoresis
  • Parenteral iron only when oral fails or cannot be absorbed
exam_pearl: Microcytic anemia not improving on oral iron: check adherence and dosing first, then think thalassemia trait (normal RDW, do Hb electrophoresis); it is not an automatic switch to IV iron.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1443).
Compiler note: Bold option in screenshot (top of next page); photo of toenails with koilonychia.

stem: A 30 minute neonate at 27 weeks, delivered by emergency cesarean section for maternal reason have tachypnea, lobeared breathing and chest wall recession. Blood pressure 55/35 mmHg, Heart rate 135 /min, Respiratory rate 65/min, Temperature 36.2 C, Oxygen saturation 86 %. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 27 week preterm neonate at 30 minutes of life with tachypnea (RR 65), labored breathing, chest wall recession and SpO2 86% has respiratory distress syndrome. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency in the immature lung and presents with severe distress from birth. The severity and the extreme prematurity outweigh the cesarean delivery clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumothorax is suggested by sudden deterioration, asymmetric breath sounds or ventilation; here distress is present from birth with no air leak clue.
B. Apnea of prematurity means pauses in breathing, usually starting after the first day or two, not continuous tachypnea with recession at 30 minutes.
D. TTN is a term cesarean baby with milder distress and fluid in the fissures on CXR that resolves on its own; severe hypoxia in a 27 week infant points to RDS.
key_concept:
Preterm + distress from birth + hypoxia = RDS; term C section + mild distress = TTN.
  • RDS: surfactant deficiency; CXR diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular)
  • TTN: retained fetal lung fluid; CXR perihilar streaks, fluid in fissure; self limiting
  • Antenatal corticosteroids are given to prevent RDS
  • Pneumothorax: sudden worsening, asymmetric chest
exam_pearl: C section is the TTN clue, but extreme prematurity with marked hypoxia overrides it in favor of RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Bold option in screenshot; neonatal CXR shown.

stem: 9 month boy on breast feeding , his mother recently started to introduce solid food , but he is mainly on breast feeding , what you recommend regarding his feeding:
OptD: speed up the rate of introduction of the solid food.
why_right: Iron stores from birth are largely used up by around 6 months, and breast milk contains little iron. A 9 month old who is still mainly breastfed with solids only just started is therefore at risk of iron deficiency, so iron supplementation is recommended until iron rich complementary foods are established. This is also why anemia screening is done at 9 to 12 months.
why_wrong_block:
B. Folate deficiency is uncommon in breastfed infants and routine folate supplementation is not recommended; folate is a pregnancy supplement for the mother.
C. Vitamin D is recommended for breastfed infants from birth as routine prophylaxis, but the specific risk this stem highlights (late, slow weaning at 9 months) is iron depletion.
D. Solids should be introduced gradually, one new food a few days apart to watch for reactions; rushing the pace does not reliably fix iron intake and is not the recommended advice.
key_concept:
Mainly breastfed infant beyond 6 months with limited solids = iron supplement.
  • Neonatal iron stores deplete by about 4 to 6 months
  • Breast milk is low in iron (and vitamin D)
  • Cow's milk before 12 months also causes IDA (occult GI loss, poor absorption)
  • CBC anemia screening at 9 to 12 months
  • Introduce each new food a few days apart
exam_pearl: If the stem stresses delayed or limited solids in a breastfed infant past 6 months, the answer is iron; vitamin D is the routine from birth answer.

stem: Patient with resistant hypertension associated with palpitations, sweating, and headaches. Most definitive treatment?
why_right: "Resistant hypertension" with the triad of palpitations, sweating and headaches is the classic picture of pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine secreting adrenal tumour. The lead-in asks for the most definitive treatment: surgical removal of the tumour (adrenalectomy, usually laparoscopic) is the only cure. It is done after preoperative alpha blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine), with a beta blocker added only once alpha blockade is established.
why_wrong_block: A. Renal artery stenting treats renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis: resistant hypertension, abdominal bruit, asymmetrical kidneys, rise in creatinine on ACE inhibitor). It does not explain episodic adrenergic symptoms like sweating and palpitations.
key_concept:
Pheochromocytoma: triad of headache, sweating, palpitations with (paroxysmal or resistant) hypertension.
  • Diagnosis: plasma free or 24 h urine metanephrines/catecholamines, then CT/MRI adrenal
  • Initial BP control: alpha blocker (phenoxybenzamine) first
  • Beta blocker only after alpha blockade (risk of unopposed alpha crisis)
  • Definitive: adrenalectomy
  • Renal artery stenosis: bruit, small kidney, no adrenergic spells → angioplasty/stenting
exam_pearl: "Initial / control BP" = alpha blocker; "definitive / cure" = adrenalectomy; a beta blocker first is the classic wrong answer.

stem: I had a question today about a 2-year-old kid who came with his mother. The chief complaint was that the kid's grandpa, who lives with them in the same house, was diagnosed with open tuberculosis. She's asking what we should do for the baby. The baby's medical history was almost positive for BCG vaccine.
OptA: Reassure because he already had the vaccine
OptB: Do chest X-ray and PPD and then wait for results.
OptC: Start them on isoniazid and ethambutol and typical TB treatment.
OptD: CXR + PPD + Start Latent TB Treatment NOW
why_right: A 2 year old living in the same house as a grandparent with open (infectious) TB is a high risk contact: young children progress quickly to severe disease such as TB meningitis or miliary TB. They are screened with CXR and tuberculin test to exclude active disease, and preventive (latent TB) therapy is started without waiting for the skin test result, because the test may be falsely negative early after exposure. BCG does not reliably prevent infection.
why_wrong_block:
A. BCG mainly reduces severe childhood forms of TB and does not prevent infection after close household exposure, so reassurance alone is unsafe.
B. Waiting for PPD results delays protection in a child under 5; the early test can be negative during the window period, so prophylaxis is started now and the test repeated later.
C. Multidrug therapy is for active TB, which has not been shown here (asymptomatic contact, CXR not yet done); this would be right if the CXR or symptoms showed active disease.
key_concept:
Child under 5 exposed to infectious TB: exclude active disease and start preventive therapy immediately.
  • Active TB on CXR or symptoms: full multidrug regimen
  • No active TB: latent TB regimen (e.g. isoniazid 6 months, rifampicin 4 months)
  • Recent contacts: TST ≥ 5 mm counts as positive
  • Initial negative TST in a young contact: continue prophylaxis and retest later
  • BCG history does not change contact management
exam_pearl: In young child contacts, do not wait for the PPD before starting prophylaxis; a prior BCG is never a reason to reassure.

stem: Child presented with fever, diarrhea, sunken eyes, poor feeding, hypotension, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which single finding most strongly indicates immediate admission?
why_right: Fever, diarrhea, sunken eyes and poor feeding describe dehydration, but hypotension with a capillary refill of 4 seconds shows impaired perfusion, i.e. shock. Prolonged capillary refill is the single listed finding that marks circulatory compromise, which needs admission and immediate IV fluid resuscitation rather than oral rehydration at home.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reduced appetite for solids is common in any sick child; only inability to take fluids or persistent vomiting would push toward admission.
B. Fever is a nonspecific feature of the infection and alone does not indicate severity or need for admission.
key_concept:
In pediatric dehydration, signs of poor perfusion (prolonged capillary refill over 2 s, weak pulse, hypotension, altered consciousness) mean severe dehydration or shock: admit and give IV boluses.
  • Mild: alert, normal eyes and pulse, skin pinch returns immediately
  • Moderate: irritable, sunken eyes, dry tongue, rapid pulse, slow skin pinch
  • Severe: drowsy, very sunken eyes, weak thready pulse, very slow skin pinch, scanty urine
  • Hypotension is a late sign in children
exam_pearl: In children, perfusion signs (capillary refill, pulse, mental state) outrank fever or appetite when deciding admission.

stem: Patient with bowel obstruction. Most appropriate investigation?
why_right: The lead-in is "most appropriate investigation" for bowel obstruction, not the initial one. CT abdomen with contrast is the confirmatory test: it confirms obstruction, finds the transition point and cause (adhesion, hernia, tumour, volvulus) and detects strangulation or ischemia that would need urgent surgery. Plain X-ray is only the first screening film.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal X-ray is the initial test (dilated loops, air-fluid levels) but it cannot show the cause or ischemia; it is the answer when the question says "best initial".
B. Ultrasound is limited by gas-filled bowel in adults; it is the first choice in young children (intussusception) or pregnancy.
D. Colonoscopy is not used to diagnose acute obstruction (insufflation risks perforation); it is used later, e.g. to evaluate a suspected colonic tumour or to decompress sigmoid volvulus.
key_concept:
Bowel obstruction imaging ladder:
  • Initial: erect CXR (free air) + supine/upright abdominal X-ray
  • Confirmatory/most appropriate: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
  • Child with suspected intussusception: ultrasound first
  • Peritonitis or strangulation: laparotomy, do not delay for imaging
exam_pearl: "Initial" = X-ray; "most appropriate/confirm/cause" = CT with contrast.

stem: Patient with bowel obstruction. Best initial investigation?
why_right: The lead-in is "best initial investigation". Plain abdominal X-ray (supine and upright, with an erect chest X-ray for free air) is cheap, fast and shows dilated loops and air-fluid levels, so it is the first test in suspected bowel obstruction. CT then follows to confirm the cause and look for complications.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT abdomen is the confirmatory, most informative test; it is the answer when the question asks "most appropriate" or "confirm", not "initial".
C. Ultrasound is poor in adults because bowel gas blocks the view; it is the initial test in toddlers (intussusception) or pregnancy.
key_concept:
Initial vs confirmatory in bowel obstruction:
  • Initial: abdominal X-ray + erect CXR
  • Confirmatory: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast
  • SBO on X-ray: central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes
  • LBO on X-ray: peripheral dilated colon with haustra
  • Child: ultrasound first
exam_pearl: Same disease, different verb: "best initial" = X-ray, "most appropriate" = CT.

stem: Female in her 50s or 70s with localized LLQ tenderness and pain. Most appropriate investigation?
why_right: An older woman ("50s or 70s") with localized LLQ tenderness and pain is acute diverticulitis until proven otherwise. CT abdomen with contrast is the investigation of choice: it confirms the diagnosis and shows complications such as abscess or perforation, which decide management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is avoided in acute diverticulitis (perforation risk); it is done 6 to 8 weeks after recovery to exclude colon cancer.
C. Plain X-ray only shows free air or obstruction; it cannot diagnose diverticulitis or its abscess.
D. Ultrasound is operator dependent and less accurate for diverticulitis; it is preferred for gynecologic causes, pregnancy or children.
key_concept:
Diverticulitis: older patient + LLQ pain/tenderness ± fever, change in bowel habit.
  • Investigation of choice: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Uncomplicated: antibiotics/supportive care
  • Abscess: percutaneous (image guided) drainage
  • Perforation with peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks after the attack
exam_pearl: Colonoscopy is right only AFTER the attack settles; during the acute attack the answer is CT.

stem: Female with rapidly enlarging 5 cm breast mass. Biopsy showed stromal cells with increased mitotic figures. Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: stromal cells with increased mitotic figures
key_concept:
Fibroadenoma vs phyllodes vs carcinoma:
  • Fibroadenoma: young, small, slow growth, bland stroma
  • Phyllodes: rapid growth, large, cellular stroma with mitoses, leaf-like pattern
  • Phyllodes spreads hematogenously, not to axillary nodes
  • Phyllodes treatment: wide local excision with at least 1 cm margins; mastectomy if very large
  • Carcinoma: malignant epithelial cells, older age, fixed hard mass
exam_pearl: "Stromal" + "mitoses" + "rapidly enlarging" are phyllodes words; carcinoma is defined by abnormal epithelial cells.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Female with long history of autoimmune thyroiditis developed thyroid malignancy. Most likely type?
why_right: A long history of autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is the classic risk factor for primary thyroid lymphoma (usually B-cell non-Hodgkin), which arises from the chronic lymphocytic infiltrate of the gland. Hashimoto carries a markedly increased relative risk of lymphoma, so this is the expected exam association.
why_wrong_block:
A. Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer overall and is also linked to Hashimoto, but it is the second association taught; it is the answer when the stem gives radiation exposure, a solitary nodule with lymph node spread, or psammoma bodies.
B. Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, is linked to MEN 2/RET mutation and raised calcitonin, not to autoimmune thyroiditis.
C. Anaplastic carcinoma is a rapidly growing tumour of elderly patients, often arising from long-standing goiter or differentiated cancer; it has no specific link to Hashimoto.
key_concept:
Thyroid cancer association map:
  • Hashimoto → lymphoma (classic), then papillary
  • Radiation, lymphatic spread → papillary
  • Hematogenous spread (bone, lung, liver) → follicular
  • Calcitonin, MEN 2 → medullary
  • Elderly, rapid hard mass, poor prognosis → anaplastic
exam_pearl: Hashimoto + rapid enlargement (± B symptoms) = lymphoma; Hashimoto alone can still tempt you toward papillary.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of a progressive anterior neck swelling with stridor. She has a 12-year history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Physical examination confirmed a diffuse, large, non-tender thyroid swelling with retrosternal extension. A core needle biopsy was ordered (see reports). Ultrasound: Diffuse thyroid enlargement, encasing bilateral carotid sheaths. Histopathology: Malignant thyroid tumour. Which of the following is the most likely tumour?
highlight_terms_source: progressive anterior neck swelling with stridor
why_right: A woman with a 12-year history of Hashimoto thyroiditis now has a 3-month progressive, diffuse goiter with stridor, retrosternal extension and encasement of both carotid sheaths, and the biopsy is malignant. Rapid diffuse enlargement in a long-standing Hashimoto gland is the classic presentation of primary thyroid lymphoma, the malignancy most strongly associated with autoimmune thyroiditis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Follicular carcinoma presents as a solitary nodule in a normal-sized gland and spreads hematogenously (bone, lung); it does not cause rapid diffuse enlargement in a Hashimoto gland.
B. Medullary carcinoma is a C-cell tumour with raised calcitonin and MEN 2 links, usually a nodule rather than a diffuse goiter.
C. Anaplastic carcinoma also grows fast with compressive symptoms, but it typically affects elderly patients with a long-standing goiter and is a hard, fixed mass; the Hashimoto background points to lymphoma instead.
key_concept:
Rapidly growing thyroid mass with compression:
  • Background Hashimoto, diffuse enlargement → lymphoma (core biopsy, chemotherapy ± radiotherapy)
  • Elderly, long-standing goiter, hard fixed mass → anaplastic
  • Lymphoma is very responsive to treatment, anaplastic has very poor prognosis
exam_pearl: Rapid growth alone points to both lymphoma and anaplastic; the Hashimoto history is the tie-breaker for lymphoma.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presented with a recent rapid enlargement of a neck swelling associated with weight loss. She was diagnosed 25 years ago with Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis diagnosed 25 years ago now has recent rapid enlargement of the neck swelling with weight loss (a B symptom). Long-standing autoimmune thyroiditis plus rapid growth and constitutional symptoms is the textbook picture of primary thyroid lymphoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemorrhagic goiter (bleed into a nodule or cyst) causes sudden, often painful enlargement over hours to days, without weight loss or a link to Hashimoto.
C. Papillary carcinoma is usually a slow-growing nodule ± cervical nodes; rapid diffuse growth with B symptoms is not its typical course.
D. Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful, tender gland after a viral illness, fever, transient hyperthyroidism and raised ESR; it is not linked to long-standing Hashimoto or weight loss from malignancy.
key_concept:
Neck swelling in a patient with Hashimoto:
  • Rapid enlargement + B symptoms (weight loss, fever, night sweats) → thyroid lymphoma
  • Sudden painful swelling over hours → hemorrhage into a nodule
  • Painful tender gland after URTI, high ESR → subacute thyroiditis
  • Diagnosis of lymphoma: core or open biopsy (FNA often insufficient)
exam_pearl: Weight loss in a long-standing Hashimoto patient with a growing goiter = lymphoma, not just a bigger goiter.

stem: Initial treatment for Hirschsprung disease?
why_right: The lead in is initial treatment. A child presenting with Hirschsprung obstruction is first stabilized: bowel decompression (rectal irrigations or washouts, nasogastric decompression), IV fluids and correction of electrolytes, with antibiotics if enterocolitis is present. Definitive surgery (resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull through) follows once the child is stable and the diagnosis is confirmed by rectal biopsy.
why_wrong_block: A. Surgical resection of the aganglionic segment is the definitive treatment, done electively after decompression and biopsy confirmation, not as an immediate first step; a total colectomy is not the standard operation.
key_concept:
Hirschsprung: decompress and stabilize first, then definitive pull through resection.
  • Clues: delayed meconium beyond 24 to 48 h, distension, bilious vomiting
  • DRE: tight sphincter, empty rectum, explosive gush of stool (squirt sign)
  • Initial imaging: AXR or contrast enema (transition zone)
  • Confirmatory test: rectal biopsy (absent ganglion cells)
  • Enterocolitis: fluids, decompression, antibiotics
exam_pearl: Read the verb: "initial" = decompression and support; "definitive" or "most appropriate management" = surgical resection.

stem: Child with enlarged tonsils and exudate. Brother also sick. Associated runny nose and conjunctivitis present. Most likely diagnosis?
key_concept:
Exudate alone does not separate viral from bacterial tonsillitis; the companions decide. The companion recall with this same scenario (AS-2068) is keyed to adenovirus pharyngitis.
  • Conjunctivitis + coryza + family cluster: adenovirus
  • Tender anterior nodes, no cough or coryza: group A strep
  • Generalized nodes, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes: EBV
  • Strep confirmed by rapid antigen test or throat culture
exam_pearl: Conjunctivitis plus runny nose pushes exudative tonsillitis toward a virus; their absence with tender anterior nodes favors strep.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer printed; see 2068 (same scenario, answer Adenovirus pharyngitis).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 5 year old child has red eye, headache, sore throat, and fever. On examination the patient has bilateral conjunctivitis and tonsillitis with exudates. His 2 year old brother had the same symptoms 2 days ago. What IS the likely cause? (No lymph node, no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly. no GI symptoms were mentioned)
highlight_terms_source: 2 year old brother had the same symptoms
why_right: Fever, sore throat and exudative tonsillitis together with bilateral conjunctivitis in a 5 year old, with a 2 year old brother who had the same illness 2 days earlier, is pharyngoconjunctival fever caused by adenovirus. Adenovirus spreads easily within households and causes conjunctivitis, pharyngitis and fever at any age. The absence of lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly argues against EBV.
why_wrong_block:
A. Kawasaki disease needs fever for 5 days or more with non exudative conjunctivitis, lip and tongue changes, extremity changes, rash or a cervical node; exudative tonsillitis and a sibling cluster point to infection instead.
B. Group A strep causes exudative tonsillitis with tender anterior nodes but not conjunctivitis; the conjunctivitis and rapid spread to a 2 year old favor a virus.
D. Infectious mononucleosis gives exudative tonsillitis with prominent lymphadenopathy, fatigue and often hepatosplenomegaly, mostly in adolescents; none of these are present and conjunctivitis is not typical.
key_concept:
Exudative tonsillitis + conjunctivitis + household spread = adenovirus (pharyngoconjunctival fever); management is supportive.
  • Adenovirus: conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, fever, gastroenteritis, croup, cystitis, pneumonia
  • Strep: tender anterior nodes, no cough or conjunctivitis
  • EBV: generalized nodes, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes
  • Kawasaki: fever ≥ 5 days, conjunctivitis without exudate, mucosal and extremity changes
exam_pearl: Conjunctivitis with exudative tonsillitis is adenovirus; conjunctivitis without exudate and prolonged fever is Kawasaki.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (originally numbered 32) on next page; answer printed below options.

stem: Unvaccinated infant with meningitis. Gram-negative pleomorphic coccobacillus identified. Organism?
why_right: A gram negative pleomorphic coccobacillus in the CSF identifies Haemophilus influenzae. In an unvaccinated infant this is type b (Hib), which was a leading cause of infant meningitis before the Hib conjugate vaccine. The vaccination history is the second clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neisseria meningitidis is a gram negative diplococcus (kidney bean pairs), often with a petechial or purpuric rash; it is not a pleomorphic coccobacillus.
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram positive lancet shaped diplococcus; it is the commonest cause in vaccinated children and adults but does not match this Gram stain.
key_concept:
CSF Gram stain identifies the bacterium.
  • Gram negative coccobacilli: H. influenzae type b (unvaccinated)
  • Gram negative diplococci: N. meningitidis
  • Gram positive diplococci: S. pneumoniae
  • Gram positive rods: Listeria (neonates, elderly, immunocompromised)
  • Hib contacts: rifampicin prophylaxis
exam_pearl: Coccobacillus = Haemophilus; diplococcus = meningococcus (negative) or pneumococcus (positive).

stem: female 7y old with facial rash and multiple small joint tenderness suggestive of SLE. Marker of disease activity?
why_right: The question asks for a marker of disease activity, not a screening test. Anti dsDNA is specific for SLE and its titer rises with flares, particularly lupus nephritis, so it is used (with complement C3 and C4, which fall during activity) to monitor disease activity.
why_wrong_block:
A. ANA is the sensitive screening test for SLE; it stays positive regardless of activity and its titer does not track flares.
B. Rheumatoid factor is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and is nonspecific; it is neither diagnostic of nor a monitor for SLE.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies by role.
  • ANA: screening, most sensitive
  • Anti Smith: most specific
  • Anti dsDNA: specific and tracks disease activity (with low C3 and C4)
  • Anti histone: drug induced lupus
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies: thrombosis and pregnancy loss
exam_pearl: Screening = ANA, most specific = anti Smith, activity = anti dsDNA and complement.

stem: Child with severe epigastric pain, pancreatic edema on ultrasound, amylase 400 lipase 100 something, Best treatment?
why_right: Severe epigastric pain plus raised pancreatic enzymes plus pancreatic edema on ultrasound meets the 2 of 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis. Treatment is supportive: IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer lactate preferred) and adequate analgesia, with early feeding as tolerated. Nothing in the stem points to biliary obstruction or infection.
why_wrong_block: A. Antibiotics have no role in acute pancreatitis unless an infection is confirmed (e.g. infected necrosis), and ERCP is reserved for confirmed gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction; neither is described here.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3x normal, imaging findings.
  • Step 1: IV crystalloid (Ringer lactate), analgesia
  • Step 2: supportive care, early enteral feeding
  • Antibiotics: only for proven infection
  • ERCP: only biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis/obstruction
  • CT: if diagnosis unclear or to assess complications after 48 to 72 h
  • Children: trauma, drugs, viral, biliary and congenital anomalies are common causes
exam_pearl: Fluids and pain control first; ERCP and antibiotics are tempting distractors that need a specific indication.

stem: Patient with ruptured appendix and localized abscess. Most appropriate management?
why_right: A ruptured appendix that has walled off into a localized abscess is managed non-operatively first: percutaneous image-guided drainage plus IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy after the inflammation settles. Operating immediately on an inflamed, matted abscess has higher complication rates (bowel injury, ileocecal resection), which is why surgery is delayed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis or for free perforation with generalized peritonitis; with a contained abscess it risks a difficult, morbid operation.
C. Antibiotics and observation alone fit an appendiceal phlegmon (inflammatory mass without pus). A localized abscess needs the pus drained, and the classic plan then removes the appendix later because the abscess can recur and, in older patients, an underlying appendiceal or cecal tumour must be excluded.
key_concept:
Appendicitis by stage:
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon (mass, no pus): IV antibiotics, conservative
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics → interval appendectomy
  • Free perforation with generalized peritonitis: urgent appendectomy + washout
exam_pearl: Localized abscess = drain now, operate later; generalized peritonitis = operate now.

stem: Patient complaining of perianal painful lump for 12 hours. 1*1 in size, Dome shaped, Bluish in color and tender. Management?
why_right: A painful, tender, dome-shaped, bluish perianal lump of 12 hours is an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid. This recall's key is lateral internal sphincterotomy, reasoning that internal sphincter spasm drives the pain and venous congestion, so lowering the high anal resting pressure treats the cause. It is kept here as keyed; see the concern note.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conservative care (sitz baths, analgesia, stool softeners, topical agents) is the usual choice when a thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents after about 72 hours, when the pain is already settling.
B. Rubber band ligation is for grade I to III internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line; banding the somatically innervated external tissue causes severe pain.
D. Needle aspiration does not evacuate the clotted thrombus and is not a standard option; when early intervention is chosen it is excision (or incision and evacuation) of the clot.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump:
  • Thrombosed external hemorrhoid: acute, tender, bluish/purplish lump
  • Within about 72 h: excision of the thrombosed hemorrhoid under local anesthesia
  • After about 72 h: conservative
  • Lateral internal sphincterotomy: standard surgery for CHRONIC anal fissure
  • Perianal abscess: red, fluctuant, fever → incision and drainage
exam_pearl: Bluish tender lump with acute pain is a thrombosed hemorrhoid, not a fissure; sphincterotomy is the textbook fissure operation.

Most likely diagnosis/management?' A. Conservative management B. Aspiration C. Band ligation (no answer marked in typed block). Screenshot (fuller recall, used as stem) note (Arabic): answer C, memorize it; a surgeon asked and C was correct. 'Smle by hamza answered C and he got 100. Alharbi: C. C then.' stem: 4month old baby, presented with signs of UTI, stable not dehydrated. Alert and feeding we Urinalysis: Positive nitrite., Positive leukocytes., Fever: 39.1 What's the appropriate empirical antibiotic to be started?
why_right: Febrile UTI (fever 39.1, nitrite and leukocyte esterase positive) in a 4 month old who is stable, alert, feeding well and not dehydrated. Infants older than about 2 months who are not toxic and tolerate oral intake can be treated orally, with outcomes equal to IV therapy. Of the options, oral amoxicillin is the only oral agent aimed at uropathogens, so it is the keyed choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Azithromycin (a macrolide) does not reliably cover Gram negative uropathogens such as E. coli and is not used for UTI.
C. IV ceftriaxone is for infants younger than about 2 months, toxic appearance, vomiting or inability to tolerate oral intake; this infant is alert and feeding well.
D. IV cefepime is a broad spectrum antipseudomonal agent reserved for severe or resistant infection; a mild febrile UTI does not need it.
key_concept:
Pediatric febrile UTI: route depends on age and how sick the child looks.
  • Older than 2 to 3 months, well, tolerating orals: oral (cephalexin, cefixime, amoxicillin per local resistance)
  • Young infant, toxic, vomiting, dehydrated: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • Urinalysis clues: nitrite, leukocyte esterase, pyuria
  • Gold standard: urine culture (catheter or suprapubic sample)
exam_pearl: Same infant but vomiting, lethargic or under 2 months flips the answer to IV ceftriaxone.

stem: Patient involved in RTA with air in the chest and neck/ after trauma. Most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: air in the chest and neck
why_right: After blunt chest trauma (RTA), "air in the chest and neck" means air has escaped from the lung into the pleural space (pneumothorax) and tracked into the soft tissues of the neck (subcutaneous emphysema). A rib fracture puncturing the lung is the commonest mechanism, so pneumothorax is the most likely diagnosis. Expect reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance and crepitus over the chest wall and neck.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aortic injury: deceleration injury that shows a widened mediastinum and hypotension, not free air in the chest and neck.
C. Pulmonary embolism: a clot in the pulmonary arteries causing sudden dyspnea and hypoxia, usually days after trauma or immobility; it never produces air in the tissues.
D. Cardiac contusion: blunt injury to the myocardium presenting with arrhythmias or ECG changes and troponin rise, not with air leak.
key_concept:
Air in the chest after trauma = pneumothorax until proven otherwise.
  • Air + crepitus in neck/chest wall = subcutaneous emphysema from lung leak
  • Tension: trachea shifted away, raised JVP, hypotension, hyperresonance
  • Tension treatment: needle decompression then chest tube
  • Simple pneumothorax treatment: chest tube
  • Persistent large air leak + pneumomediastinum: think tracheobronchial injury
exam_pearl: Air in tissues points to a leak from lung or airway; widened mediastinum points to the aorta; raised JVP with equal air entry points to tamponade.

stem: Following a head-on motor vehicle collision, a 21-year-old unrestrained passenger presents to ER with dyspnea and respiratory distress. She is intubated and physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema and decreased breath sounds. Chest x-ray reveals cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum, and a right-sided pneumothorax. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A head-on (deceleration) collision with respiratory distress, subcutaneous and cervical emphysema, pneumomediastinum and a pneumothorax together is the classic picture of a tracheobronchial injury. The disrupted airway leaks air into the mediastinum, neck and pleura at the same time, usually near the carina. Clues that confirm it in practice are a persistent large air leak or a lung that fails to re-expand after a chest tube; bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tension pneumothorax: explains the pneumothorax but not the pneumomediastinum and cervical emphysema; it would show tracheal shift, raised JVP and hypotension.
B. Open pneumothorax: requires an open chest wall wound (sucking chest wound), which is absent after this blunt injury.
D. Esophageal injury: can also cause pneumomediastinum, but it is rare in blunt trauma and presents with chest pain, dysphagia and sepsis (or follows vomiting in Boerhaave), not immediate respiratory distress with pneumothorax.
E. Pulmonary contusion: bruised lung causing hypoxia with patchy opacities on X-ray; it does not cause free air in the mediastinum or neck.
key_concept:
Air everywhere (neck + mediastinum + pleura) after blunt deceleration = tracheobronchial injury.
  • Persistent air leak or non-expanding lung after chest tube = suspect airway tear
  • Diagnosis: bronchoscopy
  • Esophageal perforation: pneumomediastinum + chest pain/vomiting, contrast leak on esophagography
  • Tension pneumothorax: tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension
  • Open pneumothorax: chest wall defect
  • Pulmonary contusion: hypoxia + opacities, no free air
exam_pearl: Pneumothorax alone = lung leak; pneumothorax plus pneumomediastinum plus neck emphysema after blunt trauma = airway rupture.

stem: A 6-year-old child is complaining that he cannot see the board in his classroom. He was diagnosed with Hypermetropia. Which of the following is the best next step?
OptD: Cover one eye / Contact lenses / Artificial tears
why_right: The card states the child "was diagnosed with Hypermetropia". In hypermetropia the eye is too short, so light focuses behind the retina; a convex (plus) lens converges light to bring the focus onto the retina. Symptomatic hypermetropia in a school-age child is corrected with convex spectacles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits mild asymptomatic hypermetropia in young children; this child is symptomatic, so correction is needed.
B. Concave (minus) lenses diverge light and correct myopia, where the image focuses in front of the retina.
D. Patching treats amblyopia (after refractive correction), contact lenses are not first line in a young child, and artificial tears treat dry eye.
key_concept:
Lens rule: Hypermetropia = convex (plus); Myopia = concave (minus).
  • Myopia: eye too long, blurred DISTANCE vision (cannot see the board)
  • Hypermetropia: eye too short, near vision worse, eye strain, risk of convergent squint and amblyopia
  • Astigmatism: cylindrical lens
  • Presbyopia: convex reading glasses
exam_pearl: "Cannot see the board" usually means myopia; follow the diagnosis stated in the stem to pick the lens.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version: 'Preschool child with hypermetropia. What you will do?' A. Concave glasses B. Convex glasses C. Covered one eye; Answer: B. 'Q:' fuller version Answer: Convex lenses.

stem: A patient came to the ER with multiple fractures and was given crystalloids but continued bleeding profusely. Labs showed Hb < 7 g/dL and severe tachycardia. The source of bleeding was not mentioned. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: The patient keeps bleeding profusely despite crystalloids, with Hb < 7 g/dL and severe tachycardia: a non-responder in hemorrhagic shock. Ongoing hemorrhage in an unstable trauma patient needs immediate operative control, and the abdomen is the commonest hidden source, so surgical laparotomy is the most appropriate next step among these options. Unstable patients go to the operating room, not to further tests or laparoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABG: may support the assessment of shock but does nothing to stop the bleeding and delays definitive control.
B. Diagnostic laparoscopy: reserved for stable patients with an unclear diagnosis; pneumoperitoneum worsens hemodynamics in shock and the view is poor with massive bleeding.
key_concept:
Unstable trauma patient with ongoing bleeding = control the hemorrhage surgically.
  • Non-responder to fluids = active bleeding, needs blood products + operative control
  • Stable patient: CT to define injuries
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy, never CT or laparoscopy
  • Pelvic fracture source: binder, then angioembolization or packing
  • Chest source: chest tube, thoracotomy if output criteria met
exam_pearl: Instability is the decision point: stable goes to the scanner, unstable goes to the operating room.

stem: 4-year-old comes with 1 month history of non-bloody diarrhea, it only occurs in daytime and not at night, the patient appears well and no failure to thrive.
highlight_terms_source: only occurs in daytime and not at night
why_right: Chronic (1 month) non-bloody loose stools in a 4-year-old who looks well with no failure to thrive, occurring in the daytime and not at night, is the classic picture of toddler's diarrhea (functional diarrhea). It is linked to high fruit juice and low fat intake and settles with dietary advice; growth stays normal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rotavirus causes acute watery diarrhea with vomiting and fever, mainly under 2 years, lasting days rather than a month.
C. Salmonella causes acute febrile diarrhea, often with blood or mucus and systemic upset, not a month of daytime-only stools in a well child.
key_concept:
Chronic diarrhea in a thriving child = functional until proven otherwise.
  • Toddler's diarrhea: 1 to 5 years, daytime only, undigested food in stool, normal growth
  • Celiac: failure to thrive, distension, buttock wasting after gluten
  • IBD: weight loss, blood, nocturnal symptoms
  • Infective (rota, salmonella): acute, febrile
exam_pearl: Nocturnal diarrhea or poor growth points away from toddler's diarrhea toward organic disease.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed version lists only A. Toddler's diarrhea B. Rotavirus with no answer; embedded screenshot gives Answer: A.

stem: A 2-year-old child initially had upper respiratory tract infection / viral symptoms. After around 12 hours, the child presented to the ER with cyanosis, drooling, tripod position, and oxygen saturation of 88%. What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: upper respiratory tract infection / viral symptoms
why_right: This recall's key is bacterial tracheitis because the child first had viral URTI symptoms and then deteriorated over hours to severe obstruction (cyanosis, SpO2 88%, tripod posture). Bacterial tracheitis is a secondary bacterial infection (often S. aureus) of the trachea following a viral illness or croup, producing thick purulent membranes and a toxic child who does not respond to croup treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Croup gives barking cough and stridor in a usually well looking child after a URTI; cyanosis, drooling and tripod position are not expected and would signal failure.
B. Epiglottitis classically gives drooling, tripod position and toxicity, but it starts abruptly in a previously well child without a viral prodrome and is now rare after Hib vaccination.
key_concept:
Upper airway emergencies in children:
  • Croup: viral prodrome, barking cough, stridor, well looking
  • Bacterial tracheitis: viral prodrome then sudden toxic deterioration, poor response to epinephrine
  • Epiglottitis: abrupt high fever, drooling, tripod, muffled voice, no cough
  • All severe cases: secure airway first
exam_pearl: Viral prodrome then sudden toxic decline = tracheitis; abrupt onset with drooling in a previously well child = epiglottitis.

stem: A pediatric patient came to the well clinic with only runny nose and cough. Temperature was 36.5°C. What should be done regarding vaccination?
why_right: The child has only a runny nose and cough with a normal temperature (36.5°C). A mild illness with or without low grade fever is not a contraindication to any vaccine, including live vaccines, so the scheduled vaccines should be given today. Postponing only creates missed opportunities.
why_wrong_block:
B. Postponing is for a moderate or severe acute illness (e.g. high fever, ill child); a simple cold does not justify delay.
C. Withholding live vaccines is for immunosuppression or pregnancy (and timing after blood products), not for a minor URTI.
key_concept:
Vaccinate unless there is a true contraindication or precaution.
  • Give: mild URTI, low grade fever, antibiotics, recent exposure, prematurity
  • Postpone: moderate to severe acute illness
  • Contraindicated: anaphylaxis to prior dose or component
  • Avoid live vaccines: immunocompromise, pregnancy
exam_pearl: A cold is not a reason to delay vaccination; only moderate to severe illness is.

stem: Patient came complaining of bleeding with and after defecation with mild itching, what's the cause:
why_right: Bleeding with and after defecation without any mention of pain, plus mild itching, is the typical picture of internal hemorrhoids. They bleed bright red blood on the stool or paper and commonly cause pruritus and mucus discharge. The absence of sharp pain, swelling, fever or chronic discharge rules out the other options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure: also bleeds bright red blood, but the key feature is sharp, severe pain during and after defecation, usually with constipation.
B. Perianal abscess: a painful, tender perianal swelling with fever and leukocytosis, not bleeding with stool.
D. Fistula: presents with persistent perianal discharge from an external opening, often after a previous abscess, not bleeding with defecation.
key_concept:
Anorectal complaint by its dominant symptom:
  • Painless bright red bleeding (± itching) = hemorrhoids
  • Painful bleeding on defecation = fissure (midline, 6 or 12 o'clock)
  • Painful swelling + fever + leukocytosis = abscess
  • Chronic discharge = fistula
  • Painful tender purplish lump = thrombosed external hemorrhoid
exam_pearl: Pain is the switch: the same bright red bleeding is a fissure if it hurts and hemorrhoids if it does not.

stem: A patient has a thyroid mass and laboratory results show a markedly elevated serum calcitonin level 48. This finding is most consistent with which type of thyroid cancer?
why_right: Calcitonin is made by the parafollicular C cells, and medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from these cells. A thyroid mass with an elevated serum calcitonin therefore points to medullary carcinoma, and calcitonin (with CEA) is also its tumor marker for follow-up. Treatment is total thyroidectomy, and MEN 2 (RET mutation) should be considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Papillary carcinoma: arises from follicular cells, spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes, and is followed with thyroglobulin, not calcitonin.
B. Follicular carcinoma: also a follicular cell tumor followed with thyroglobulin; it spreads hematogenously to bone, lung and liver.
D. Anaplastic carcinoma: a rapidly growing hard mass in an elderly patient with compressive symptoms; it is not a calcitonin secreting tumor.
key_concept:
Match the thyroid cancer to its cell and marker:
  • Medullary: C cells, calcitonin (and CEA), MEN 2/RET, total thyroidectomy
  • Papillary: follicular cells, lymphatic spread, thyroglobulin
  • Follicular: follicular cells, hematogenous spread, thyroglobulin
  • Anaplastic: elderly, rapid growth, compression, poor prognosis
  • Hashimoto + rapidly enlarging goiter: think thyroid lymphoma
exam_pearl: Calcitonin = medullary; thyroglobulin = papillary or follicular.

stem: 7 year-old child unvaccinated presents with mild fever and cropped vesicles on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis? Vitals weren't given
why_right: An unvaccinated child with mild fever and vesicles appearing in crops on the trunk (central distribution, lesions at different stages) is chickenpox caused by varicella zoster virus. It is a clinical diagnosis, confirmable by PCR if needed.
why_wrong_block:
B. HSV-1 in children causes gingivostomatitis: painful vesicles and ulcers on the lips, gums and mouth with cervical nodes, not crops of truncal vesicles.
C. Smallpox is eradicated; its lesions were all at the same stage and concentrated on the face and limbs (centrifugal).
D. Measles gives a maculopapular (not vesicular) rash starting on the face with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
key_concept:
Vesicular rash in a child:
  • Varicella: crops, different stages, starts on trunk/face then spreads, itchy
  • Smallpox: same stage, centrifugal, deep lesions
  • HSV-1: perioral and gingival vesicles
  • Hand foot mouth: oral ulcers plus hands and feet
  • Measles: maculopapular, Koplik spots
exam_pearl: Lesions at different stages = varicella; all at the same stage = smallpox.

stem: Child present with meconium aspiration and shortness of breath, was managed by mechanical intubation. how to diagnose complications?
why_right: Meconium aspiration requiring mechanical ventilation is a classic setting for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), with right-to-left shunting through the ductus and foramen ovale. The diagnostic test for this complication is echocardiography, which shows raised pulmonary pressures and the shunt and excludes structural heart disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bronchoscopy is not used to diagnose complications of meconium aspiration; it has a role mainly for suspected airway foreign body or structural airway lesions.
C. Lung ultrasound can show parenchymal changes or pneumothorax but cannot assess pulmonary artery pressure or ductal shunting.
D. ECG may show right ventricular strain but is neither sensitive nor specific for PPHN.
key_concept:
Complications of meconium aspiration and how to find them:
  • PPHN: pre-ductal SpO2 higher than post-ductal, confirm by echo, treat with inhaled nitric oxide
  • Pneumothorax (air leak on ventilation): chest X-ray
  • Chemical pneumonitis, surfactant inactivation
exam_pearl: Pre/post-ductal saturation gap in a ventilated meconium baby = PPHN; confirm with echo.

stem: A 30 year old male presented with foul smelling of perianal discharge. No change in bowel habits, no bleeding no diarrhea. On examination, 3 perianal fistulas were found on 7 and 3 o'clock and maybe 11 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: No change in bowel habits, no bleeding no diarrhea
why_right: This recall's key is pelvic MRI because the patient has multiple perianal fistulas (3 openings) with foul discharge, which makes them complex fistulas. Pelvic MRI is the imaging of choice to map complex tracts, their relation to the sphincters and any hidden abscess before surgery. Multiple fistulas in a young adult should also raise suspicion of Crohn's disease.
why_wrong_block:
B. Fistulogram: an outdated contrast study that poorly shows tracts in relation to the sphincters; it has been replaced by MRI.
C. Rectal US: endoanal ultrasound is an acceptable alternative where MRI is unavailable, but it is operator dependent and less accurate for complex or high tracts.
D. Colonoscopy: used to look for underlying Crohn's disease when complex fistulas occur without a known diagnosis; it does not map the fistula tracts themselves.
key_concept:
Simple vs complex perianal fistula:
  • Simple low fistula: fistulotomy
  • Complex (multiple, recurrent, high): image the tracts with pelvic MRI
  • Known Crohn's + complex fistula: MRI to assess the tract
  • Crohn's not known: colonoscopy to confirm Crohn's
  • Then antibiotics; infliximab for refractory Crohn's fistulas
exam_pearl: Multiple or recurrent fistulas are complex and possibly Crohn's: MRI maps the tract, colonoscopy looks for the cause.

stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 28-year-old with "three fistula openings", recurrent abdominal pain and a family history of Crohn's has multiple, complex perianal fistulae that point to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. This recall's key is colonoscopy (with ileoscopy and biopsies) to confirm the underlying disease, because fistula management is very different in Crohn's (medical therapy, setons, avoiding fistulotomy).
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
C. Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
D. US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.
key_concept:
Multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae: think Crohn's.
  • Suspected Crohn's not yet diagnosed: colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsy
  • Fistula anatomy or abscess: MRI pelvis
  • Abscess: drain before escalating immunosuppression
  • Fistulizing Crohn's: anti-TNF (infliximab), setons
  • Simple low non-Crohn's fistula: fistulotomy
exam_pearl: Known Crohn's with perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis; suspected but undiagnosed Crohn's: colonoscopy.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0013).
Compiler note: 'Q:' variant under 2100 with a different stem (abdominal pain, family history of Crohn's); compiler highlighted Colonoscopy.

stem: crohns disease, presented with distended bowel, but no bleeding or diarrhea (I think that's how it's written), on imaging it shows a large distended bowl (not abscess). What's the management:
key_concept:
Crohn's complication decides the management:
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Stricture with obstruction (vomiting, pain, distension): resection, stricturoplasty second line
  • Uncomplicated obstruction: start with bowel rest, NG decompression, IV fluids
  • Strangulation, perforation or instability: laparotomy
  • Perianal fistula: MRI, antibiotics, biologics
exam_pearl: No abscess on imaging removes drainage; distended bowel makes this an obstruction (stricture) question.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the ER with abnormal movements during sleep involving his face and limbs. He has a history of seizures but is otherwise neurologically normal. EEG shows frontotemporal spikes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 7-year-old, neurologically normal, with seizures during sleep involving the face (and limbs) and temporal region spikes on EEG is benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (rolandic epilepsy). It peaks in school age, usually starts focal in the face and mouth with drooling or speech arrest, may generalize at night, and remits by adolescence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Infantile spasms (West syndrome) occur in infants with clusters of flexor or extensor spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
B. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks after waking, and generalized polyspike and wave on EEG.
key_concept:
Childhood epilepsy syndromes by age and EEG:
  • Infantile spasms: infancy, hypsarrhythmia
  • Absence: 5 to 8 years, staring, 3 Hz spike and wave
  • Rolandic: school age, nocturnal facial seizures, centrotemporal spikes, normal child
  • JME: adolescence, morning myoclonus, polyspike and wave
exam_pearl: Nocturnal facial twitching in a normal school-age child = rolandic; morning jerks in a teenager = JME.

stem: A 5-day-old girl brought to Emergency Room with lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, she was irritable, deeply jaundiced and dehydrated. The mother gave history of previous babies' required admission and exchange transfusion (see lab results). Which of the following is important to be obtained in the history? Blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, Heart rate 95 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Oxygen saturation 94 %, Weight 3 kg. Hb 95 (165-195 g/L newborn); Reticulocyte 3 (0.2-1.2 %); Total bilirubin 360 (<205 mol/L term 3-5 days).
highlight_terms_source: previous babies' required admission and exchange transfusion
why_right: Day 5 neonate with deep jaundice (bilirubin 360), anemia (Hb 95) and raised reticulocytes (3%) has a hemolytic picture. Previous babies needing exchange transfusion points to recurrent isoimmune hemolytic disease, typically Rh alloimmunization worsening with each pregnancy. Maternal blood group (with the baby's group and a direct Coombs test) is the key history item.
why_wrong_block:
A. Apgar score reflects transition and asphyxia at birth; it does not explain hemolysis recurring across siblings.
B. Birth weight does not explain a familial hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
C. Type of delivery may relate to bruising or cephalohematoma, but not to recurrent hemolysis requiring exchange transfusion in siblings.
key_concept:
Neonatal jaundice plus anemia plus reticulocytosis = hemolysis.
  • Ask: maternal and baby blood groups (Rh, ABO), anti-D history
  • Test: direct Coombs
  • Rh disease: worsens in successive pregnancies
  • ABO: can affect the first baby, usually milder
  • Others: G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis
exam_pearl: Siblings who needed exchange transfusion is the classic Rh isoimmunization clue.

stem: An 80-year-old man presents with lower abdominal pain. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 1 × 1 cm fluid collection in the lower abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptB: Start empiric IV antibiotics and observe
key_concept:
Intra-abdominal collection ladder:
  • Small (below 4 × 4 cm), stable: antibiotics (conservative)
  • 4 × 4 cm or more: percutaneous (image-guided) drainage
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy
exam_pearl: Size and stability drive the choice: a 1 cm collection is never drained first.

Compiler note: No answer marked for 2106; the following item 2107 (febrile version) has Answer: B.
