stem: An 80-year-old man presents with lower abdominal pain. He is febrile and hemodynamically stable. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 1 × 1 cm fluid collection in the lower abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: The patient is febrile but hemodynamically stable, and the collection is only 1 × 1 cm. A small collection (below about 4 × 4 cm) is too small to drain and is treated non-invasively with IV antibiotics, with drainage kept for failure to respond. Fever means it is likely infected, so antibiotics rather than simple observation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate surgical drainage: reserved for collections not reachable percutaneously or failed drainage; excessive for a 1 cm collection in a stable patient.
C. CT-guided drainage: indicated for collections about 4 × 4 cm or larger, or a small one that fails antibiotics.
D. Conservative: observation alone without treatment is inadequate when fever suggests infection; this patient needs antibiotics.
key_concept:
Intra-abdominal collection ladder:
  • Small (below 4 × 4 cm), stable: IV antibiotics
  • 4 × 4 cm or more: percutaneous (image-guided) drainage
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable patient: laparotomy
exam_pearl: A big collection or failed antibiotics turns the answer to percutaneous drainage; instability turns it to laparotomy.

stem: A woman with BMI of 35 I think, type 2 DM, wants to lose weight, however she tried exercising and diet and none of them worked for her, what do you recommend for her?
OptA: Take medications that help with weight loss
highlight_terms_source: tried exercising and diet and none of them worked
why_right: She has BMI 35 with type 2 DM (an obesity-related comorbidity) and has failed diet and exercise. BMI 35 or more with comorbidities after failed lifestyle therapy meets the indication for bariatric surgery, which gives the largest durable weight loss and frequently improves or remits diabetes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Take medications that help with weight loss: a valid adjunct (for example at BMI 30, or 27 with comorbidities), but loss is modest; once BMI is 35 or more with diabetes after failed lifestyle therapy, surgery is the recommended option.
C. Diet: she has already tried diet without success; repeating it does not address her eligibility for more effective treatment.
key_concept:
Bariatric surgery indications (after failed lifestyle therapy):
  • BMI 40 or more
  • BMI 35 or more with comorbidity (T2DM, HTN, OSA)
  • Pre-op: upper GI endoscopy is the key test for choosing the procedure
  • Severe GERD or hiatal hernia: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
  • No reflux: sleeve gastrectomy
exam_pearl: BMI 35 plus type 2 DM after failed diet and exercise meets surgical criteria; drugs are the step for lower BMI (30, or 27 with comorbidity).

stem: An 18-month-old child with normal growth and weight 50th percentile is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling was recently diagnosed with celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: This recall's key is reassurance because the 18-month-old is asymptomatic with normal growth (50th percentile); a sibling's diagnosis raises risk but does not make this child ill. Screening of well first-degree relatives is usually deferred until about 2 to 3 years of age, after adequate gluten exposure, so nothing is needed today beyond reassurance and a plan to test later or sooner if symptoms appear. A gluten free diet must never be started without a confirmed diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. tTG-IgA (with total IgA) is the right first test when there are celiac symptoms (diarrhea, distension, failure to thrive), or as screening of an at-risk relative once older (about 2 to 3 years); this toddler is well and young, so testing can wait.
C. Starting a gluten free diet without serology and biopsy is wrong: it is unnecessary in a healthy child and causes false negative results if testing is later needed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease workup:
  • Symptoms or failure to thrive: tTG-IgA (with total IgA) while on gluten
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (do not stop gluten before)
  • Treatment: gluten free diet only after diagnosis
  • At-risk groups: first-degree relatives, type 1 diabetes, Down, Turner syndromes
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten free diet before testing; it masks the diagnosis.

stem: An 4-Year-Old child with normal growth and weight is brought by his parents. They are concerned because his older sibling has celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: First-degree relatives of a patient with celiac disease are at high risk and should be screened even when asymptomatic. This child with "normal growth and weight" whose "older sibling has celiac disease" should have tTG IgA, the initial screening serology, while still eating gluten.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance misses a high-risk child; normal growth does not exclude celiac disease, which can be silent in relatives.
C. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing is wrong: gluten withdrawal makes serology and biopsy falsely negative, and diet is only started after the diagnosis is confirmed.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: serology, then biopsy, then diet.
  • Screen first-degree relatives and type 1 diabetes even without symptoms
  • Initial test: tTG IgA (with total IgA)
  • Confirm: endoscopy with duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia)
  • Test while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet; tTG also monitors compliance
exam_pearl: Never start a gluten-free diet before serology and biopsy; it produces false-negative results.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0584).

stem: pt with numbness, lower limb weakness, sever back pain, MRI show abscess collection with compression sign (or something like that)
OptC: Iv antibiotics with local dressing or debridement
key_concept:
Spinal epidural abscess: neuro deficit = decompress now.
  • Classic triad: back pain, fever, neurological deficit
  • Imaging of choice: MRI with contrast
  • Deficit or progressive signs: surgical decompression + drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Neurologically intact, small collection or unfit for surgery: IV antibiotics with close monitoring
  • Any abscess elsewhere: drain it
exam_pearl: The neurological deficit is what turns an antibiotic case into an emergency surgical decompression.

stem: A 53-day-old boy is referred to the Paediatric Clinic for investigation of anaemia. He was born full term and he is a known case of G6PD deficiency. On examination, both height and weight are in the 10th percentile, the rest of the examination is normal (see lab results). Hb 70 (112-165 g/L); Platelet count 350 (150-400 x 109/L); Total bilirubin 25.1 (<20.5 mol/L). Urinalysis: Color clear; Leukocytes 0 (0-3/hpf); Erythrocytes 0 (0-2/hpf). Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: A term infant at 53 days (about 8 weeks) is at the age of the physiological Hb nadir, which falls at 8 to 12 weeks. The rest of the exam is normal and the urinalysis is clear with no blood, so there is no sign of an active hemolytic episode despite the known G6PD deficiency. The recall therefore treats this as physiological anemia of infancy, which recovers on its own as erythropoietin rises, so the keyed management is reassurance with follow up.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood transfusion: kept for a symptomatic infant (poor feeding, tachycardia, heart failure) or a severe acute hemolytic crisis; this baby is well with a normal exam. It is the main competing option because Hb 70 is lower than the usual nadir.
B. Iron supplement: a term baby has enough iron stores for the first 4 to 6 months, so iron deficiency is not the cause at 53 days; iron is right for an older infant on cow's milk with microcytosis.
D. Folic acid: there is no clue to megaloblastic anemia or folate deficiency; folate is given in chronic hemolytic states with high red cell turnover, not physiological anemia.
key_concept:
Well term infant at 8 to 12 weeks with isolated anemia and normal exam = physiological anemia of infancy: reassure and follow.
  • Term nadir: about 9 to 11 g/dL at 8 to 12 weeks
  • Preterm nadir: deeper and earlier, 3 to 6 weeks
  • Mechanism: high Hb at birth suppresses erythropoietin, then hypoxia switches it back on
  • G6PD hemolysis needs a trigger plus jaundice and dark urine
  • Term iron stores last 4 to 6 months
exam_pearl: Known G6PD deficiency is a distractor here: clear urine, no trigger and a normal exam point away from hemolysis.

stem: 6days new born with g6pd def. Type of anemia?
why_right: This recall is keyed to physiological anemia, the same teaching point as the related 53-day G6PD infant case: in a well term baby with known G6PD deficiency and no trigger, the drop in Hb is the normal postnatal fall, not disease. After birth the high fetal Hb declines because erythropoietin is suppressed by better oxygenation, and it recovers without treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hemolytic: right if there is a trigger (fava beans, infection, oxidant drugs) with jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; the known G6PD deficiency alone is the trap.
B. Inflammatory: needs an active infection or inflammatory illness, which is not described in this newborn.
C. Of chronic disease: needs a long-standing chronic illness (renal, inflammatory, malignancy); it does not fit a newborn.
key_concept:
G6PD infant with anemia but no trigger, no hemoglobinuria and a normal exam = physiological anemia, not hemolysis.
  • Term nadir at 8 to 12 weeks, Hb about 9 to 11 g/dL
  • Preterm nadir earlier (3 to 6 weeks) and deeper
  • G6PD hemolysis: trigger, jaundice, dark urine, bite or Heinz bodies
  • Neonatal G6PD often presents as early jaundice
exam_pearl: Physiological anemia is timed by age: the classic nadir is weeks 8 to 12, so check the age in the stem before choosing it.

stem: A 53-day-old boy is referred to the Paediatric Clinic for investigation of anemia. He was born at full term and he is a known case of G6PD deficiency. On examination, both height and weight are in the 10th percentile, the rest of the examination is normal (see lab results). Hb 70 (112-165 g/L); Platelet count 350 (150-400 x 109/L); Total bilirubin 25.1 (<20.5 mol/L). Urinalysis: Color clear; Leukocytes 0; Erythrocytes 0. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is the physiological option: a term boy at 53 days is at the physiological Hb nadir (8 to 12 weeks), the exam is otherwise normal and the urinalysis is clear with no blood, so the picture is a normal postnatal process rather than disease. The same case in the source is keyed to physiological anemia of infancy; read option C as that concept.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haemolysis: right with a trigger plus jaundice, pallor and dark urine or hemoglobinuria; here the urine is clear and the exam normal, so the known G6PD deficiency is a distractor.
B. Iron deficiency: term infants have adequate iron stores until about 4 to 6 months; it fits an older infant on cow's milk with low MCV.
D. Anaemia of chronic disease: needs a chronic inflammatory, renal or malignant illness, which this well infant does not have.
key_concept:
Well term infant at 8 to 12 weeks with isolated anemia = physiological anemia of infancy.
  • Term nadir: about 9 to 11 g/dL at 8 to 12 weeks
  • Physiological jaundice: starts after 24 h, resolves by about 2 weeks in term babies
  • Jaundice beyond 2 weeks (term) = prolonged, needs conjugated bilirubin
  • G6PD hemolysis: trigger, jaundice, dark urine
exam_pearl: The diagnosis being tested is physiological ANEMIA; physiological jaundice is over by 2 weeks in a term baby.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot under 2118 at top of next page (same case as 2117 but asking diagnosis); Answer: C.

stem: A 14-year-old female presents for evaluation of delayed puberty. Physical examination reveals Tanner Stage 1 for both breast development and pubic hair. Laboratory investigations show normal levels of FSH and LH, but a mildly elevated serum estradiol level. Given this clinical picture, which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
highlight_terms_source: normal levels of FSH and LH
key_concept:
Delayed puberty in a girl: first check FSH and LH.
  • High FSH/LH, low estradiol: primary ovarian failure (Turner most common)
  • Low or normal FSH/LH: constitutional delay, chronic illness, low weight, hypothalamic or pituitary causes
  • Precocious puberty: signs before age 8 in girls
  • Central = pubertal LH/FSH; peripheral = suppressed LH/FSH with high sex steroids
  • Tanner 1 breast = prepubertal
exam_pearl: Delayed (not precocious) puberty with short stature in a girl makes Turner the exam favourite, but it needs HIGH gonadotropins.

stem: 8 years old, boy bed witting No hx of UTI. What's the best next step ?
OptC: Train with a bedtime alarm or something like that. ( NO REASSURANCE )
why_right: An 8-year-old with bedwetting and no history of UTI is primary nocturnal enuresis with no red flags. Once simple behavioural measures (fluid timing, voiding before bed, rewards, no punishment) are in place, the enuresis alarm is the first-line active treatment, with the best long-term cure and lowest relapse rate. The recall also stresses that plain reassurance alone is not the answer at this age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Refer to psychiatry: enuresis is a developmental delay in bladder control, not a psychiatric illness; referral fits only when there are clear emotional or behavioural problems or abuse concerns.
B. Give Desmopressin: oral desmopressin is used when the alarm fails or is unsuitable, or for quick short-term dryness (sleepovers, camps); relapse after stopping is common, and the intranasal form is avoided because of hyponatremia.
key_concept:
Primary nocturnal enuresis, no red flags: behavioural advice, then alarm, then desmopressin.
  • Under about 5 to 6 years: reassurance
  • Behavioural: fluid timing, void before bed, star chart, no punishment
  • Alarm: best long-term cure, needs a motivated family
  • Desmopressin: oral only, short-term or alarm failure
  • Red flags (daytime symptoms, UTI, polyuria, weight loss): urinalysis and workup first
exam_pearl: Reassurance alone fits a child under about 6; an 8-year-old needs active treatment, and the alarm comes before desmopressin.

stem: 3 years old, looks acutely ill, sit on his mother's lap with his neck extended. What is the management?
why_right: A 3-year-old who looks acutely ill and sits on the mother's lap with the neck extended (sniffing or tripod posture) is acute epiglottitis until proven otherwise. The airway can obstruct completely at any moment, so the priority is to keep the child calm and secure the airway by intubation in the operating room by the most experienced anaesthetist, with ENT ready for a surgical airway. Antibiotics are given once the airway is safe.
why_wrong_block:
A. Give him racemic epinephrine: nebulized epinephrine treats moderate to severe croup (barking cough, stridor in a child who looks well); in epiglottitis it does not fix the obstruction and the procedure can upset the child and precipitate complete obstruction.
B. dexamethasone: the mainstay of croup, which presents with a barking cough after URTI symptoms in a non-toxic child; it does not secure the airway in a toxic child with epiglottitis.
key_concept:
Toxic child + drooling + sniffing/tripod posture = epiglottitis: secure the airway in the OR first.
  • Do not lie the child down, examine the throat or take blood first
  • Keep with parent, calm, give oxygen as tolerated
  • Airway by senior anaesthetist in OR, ENT on standby
  • Then IV third-generation cephalosporin
  • Croup: barking cough, looks well, dexamethasone ± nebulized epinephrine
exam_pearl: Barking cough in a well child = croup (steroids); toxic, drooling, neck extended and silent = epiglottitis (airway in the OR).

stem: 5 yrs old boy with SVT, what is the initial investigation?
why_right: The lead-in asks for the initial investigation in a child with SVT. A 12-lead ECG is first: it confirms the narrow complex regular tachycardia, guides acute treatment (vagal manoeuvres, adenosine, cardioversion if unstable), and after conversion can show a delta wave of pre-excitation (WPW); an accessory pathway (AVRT) is the commonest SVT mechanism in children.
why_wrong_block: A. Echo: done later to look for structural heart disease or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (for example in recurrent or prolonged SVT); it does not diagnose the rhythm and is not the first test.
key_concept:
Any suspected tachyarrhythmia: 12-lead ECG first, then targeted tests.
  • ECG during SVT: narrow complex, regular, P waves hidden or retrograde
  • ECG in sinus rhythm: look for delta wave (WPW)
  • Unstable: synchronized cardioversion
  • Stable: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine
  • Echo: structural disease, ventricular function
  • Holter: intermittent palpitations with a normal resting ECG
exam_pearl: Echo answers 'is the heart structurally normal'; only the ECG answers 'what is the rhythm', so it always comes first.

stem: Ruptured appendix with collection question:
key_concept:
Appendiceal or intra-abdominal collection: size and stability decide.
  • Small collection (under about 4 x 4 cm), stable: IV antibiotics
  • 4 x 4 cm or more: percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Multiple collections: laparoscopy
  • Unstable or generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Appendix abscess treated nonoperatively: interval appendectomy later
exam_pearl: Read the size: a small collection gets antibiotics only, a large one gets drained, and appendectomy waits.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Depending on the size: 4 cm -> Drain; 3 cm -> IV Abx.

stem: 7-year-old child who is the only child of his parents He refuses the school or his parents refuse "something like that" What to do?
OptA: Delay his school by one year.
why_right: A 7-year-old only child refusing school (with possibly anxious parents) suggests school refusal driven by separation anxiety. Management is behavioral: early, gradual (gentle) separation and return to school with parental support and reassurance, ideally with cognitive behavioral techniques. Avoidance reinforces the anxiety.
why_wrong_block:
A. Delay his school by one year: keeping the child away rewards avoidance and makes the anxiety worse; the goal is early return to school.
B. Study at home: again an avoidance strategy that removes the child from peers and school and entrenches the problem.
C. Give anxiety medication: drugs (SSRIs) are reserved for severe or refractory anxiety after behavioral therapy fails, not first line in a young child.
key_concept:
School refusal / separation anxiety = behavioral management, not avoidance.
  • Reassure and educate parents
  • Gradual separation and early return to school
  • CBT with exposure
  • SSRI only if severe or refractory
exam_pearl: Any option that keeps the child home (delay, home study) is wrong; graded return is the answer.

stem: A 9-year-old child with gastroenteritis caused by Shigella species. Which of the following antibiotics should be prescribed?
why_right: This recall's key is ceftriaxone: in a child with Shigella gastroenteritis, fluoroquinolones were traditionally avoided and widespread ampicillin and co-trimoxazole resistance makes older drugs unreliable, so a third-generation cephalosporin is a standard choice, particularly for severe or invasive disease or a child who cannot take oral treatment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amoxicillin: Shigella resistance to ampicillin and amoxicillin is widespread and amoxicillin is poorly effective even for sensitive strains; not recommended.
C. Azithromycin: a recognised oral option for Shigella in children and the drug of choice for Campylobacter dysentery; it is the strongest competitor here (see note).
D. Metronidazole: covers anaerobes and protozoa (Giardia, Entamoeba, C. difficile), not Shigella.
key_concept:
Bacterial dysentery: match the organism to the antibiotic.
  • Shigella, child: azithromycin (oral) or ceftriaxone (parenteral, severe)
  • Shigella, adult: ciprofloxacin
  • Campylobacter: azithromycin
  • Giardia, amoebiasis, C. difficile: metronidazole
  • Shigella clue: bloody diarrhea with fever, febrile seizures in children
exam_pearl: Bloody diarrhea plus a seizure in a child points to Shigella; metronidazole is the trap answer for Giardia.

stem: 38year old male, previous gonorrheal infection awhile ago. Cannot empty his bladder, failed transurethral catheterization. Normal urinalysis, full bladder on US. What is the most appropriate step?
highlight_terms_source: Cannot empty his bladder, failed transurethral catheterization
why_right: A young man with "previous gonorrheal infection", a full bladder on ultrasound and a "failed transurethral catheterization" has retention from a post-infective urethral stricture. The obstruction is fixed scar tissue, so it needs to be seen and opened: cystoscopy (urethroscopy) with dilation of the stricture relieves the retention and defines the stricture. A normal urinalysis rules out active infection as the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeating blind catheterization against a known stricture risks a false passage and urethral trauma. A repeat attempt suits a simple technical failure, not a fixed narrowing.
C. The gonorrhea was in the past and the urinalysis is normal; the problem is the scar it left. Antibiotics are right for active urethritis with discharge.
D. Alpha blockers relax prostatic smooth muscle and help BPH in older men; they cannot open a fibrotic urethral stricture in a 38-year-old.
key_concept:
Urinary retention with failed catheter: think about the cause.
  • Older man, enlarged prostate: Foley + urine culture, then alpha blocker
  • Previous urethritis (gonorrhea) or instrumentation: urethral stricture
  • Stricture: cystoscopy/urethroscopy with dilation or urethrotomy
  • Failed or contraindicated urethral catheter: suprapubic catheter for decompression
  • Trauma with suspected urethral injury: retrograde urethrogram first, no Foley
exam_pearl: If suprapubic catheterization is offered as an option, it is the emergency way to decompress a bladder when the urethral route fails.

stem: Painless hematuria with distended bladder and failed to insert catheter
key_concept:
Painless gross hematuria in an adult = urothelial cancer until proven otherwise.
  • Clot retention: large three-way catheter + bladder irrigation
  • Catheter fails or clots persist: cystoscopy with clot evacuation
  • Full workup: cystoscopy (bladder) + CT urography (upper tract)
  • Painful hematuria with colicky flank pain: stone
exam_pearl: Retention is the emergency; the hematuria workup comes after the bladder is decompressed.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Case of enlarged parotid gland bilaterally (it was long) what's the causative organism?
why_right: Bilateral parotid enlargement lasting for days is classic for mumps, a paramyxovirus whose most common manifestation is parotitis, often painful and starting on one side before becoming bilateral, after a short prodrome of fever and malaise. It is the commonest infectious cause of bilateral parotid swelling, especially in an unvaccinated child.
why_wrong_block:
B. EBV: causes infectious mononucleosis with exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes; parotid swelling is uncommon.
C. CMV: usually a mild mononucleosis-like illness or congenital infection (deafness, periventricular calcifications); parotitis is rare, mainly in immunocompromised patients.
key_concept:
Bilateral painful parotid swelling with fever = mumps.
  • Mumps virus: paramyxovirus, prevented by MMR
  • Complications: orchitis (post-pubertal), aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness
  • Unilateral, red, pus from Stensen duct = bacterial (S. aureus) parotitis
  • Other viral causes: parainfluenza, influenza, EBV, HIV
exam_pearl: Unilateral parotid swelling with pus from the duct in a dehydrated or postoperative patient is bacterial (S. aureus), not mumps.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A related screenshot follows on the next page (organ most commonly affected by mumps; see 2140b).

stem: Which of the following organs is most commonly affected by mumps in a 4-year-old boy?
why_right: The parotid gland is the organ most commonly affected by mumps: parotitis is its hallmark and is often bilateral and painful. In a 4-year-old (prepubertal) boy, the testes are rarely involved, so parotid clearly wins.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin: mumps does not typically cause a rash; think measles, rubella or varicella for viral rashes.
B. Lungs: pneumonia is not a feature of mumps; measles is the viral exanthem with pneumonia as a leading complication.
C. Testes: orchitis is the commonest complication in post-pubertal males (it can affect fertility), but it is rare before puberty, so it is the answer only if the stem asks about an adolescent or adult male's complication.
key_concept:
Mumps: parotitis is the most common manifestation; complications depend on age.
  • Parotitis: most common, often bilateral
  • Orchitis: mainly post-pubertal males
  • Aseptic meningitis: most common CNS involvement
  • Also pancreatitis, sensorineural deafness
  • Prevented by MMR
exam_pearl: Organ most affected = parotid; most common complication in an adult male = orchitis; read whether the stem asks for the organ or the complication.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot shown under 2140; D highlighted and 'Answer: D'.

stem: A 50-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department following a fail from 20 feet, on arrival he has a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 with no external sign of injury. Mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg Intracranial pressure 15 mmHg. Which of the following is the most likely cerebral perfusion pressure in mmHg?
why_right: Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP minus ICP. With "MAP 65 mmHg" and "ICP 15 mmHg", CPP = 65 minus 15 = 50 mmHg. The GCS of 8 and the fall are context only; the question is the calculation.
why_wrong_block:
A. 40 would need an ICP of 25 with this MAP; it comes from an arithmetic slip, not from MAP minus ICP.
C. 60 is the lower CPP target in severe head injury, a tempting number to recall, but it is not what these values give.
D. 70 would need a MAP of 85; it is the upper end of the usual CPP target range, not the calculated value.
key_concept:
CPP = MAP minus ICP.
  • MAP ≈ diastolic + one third of pulse pressure
  • Normal ICP is low; raised ICP lowers CPP
  • Severe TBI CPP target: about 60 to 70 mmHg
  • CPP of 50 here means risk of cerebral hypoperfusion
  • GCS ≤ 8: secure the airway
exam_pearl: Calculation questions: subtract ICP from MAP, do not pick the target value you remember.

stem: Patient 45 years old with right sided breast pain and bloody nipple charge, no findings on physical examination of the right breast Whats the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: Bloody nipple discharge in a "45 years old" woman needs imaging to exclude carcinoma, most often it is an intraductal papilloma. Breast imaging is chosen by age: over 30, mammogram (with or without ultrasound) is the first investigation, so with "no findings on physical examination" mammogram is the most appropriate test here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ductography is a second-line test for pathological discharge when mammogram and ultrasound show no lesion; it is not the first investigation.
C. Ultrasound is first-line under 30 (dense breasts) and in pregnancy, and complements mammogram at this age; at 45 it is not the lead test.
D. CT is used to stage distant metastasis, not to evaluate the breast itself.
key_concept:
Breast imaging is chosen by age.
  • Under 30 or pregnant: ultrasound
  • Over 30 (or strong family history): mammogram ± ultrasound
  • Most common cause of bloody discharge (non-lactating): intraductal papilloma
  • Papilloma treatment: duct excision
  • Solid mass: core needle biopsy; cyst: FNA
  • Staging distant spread: CT
exam_pearl: Same complaint in a 32-year-old is keyed to ultrasound; the age flips the first test.

stem: A patient has a postoperative open wound. The wound is improving, with healthy granulation tissue forming and no signs of infection. What is the next best management?
why_right: The wound is already "improving, with healthy granulation tissue" and "no signs of infection", so it is healing well by secondary intention. Nothing needs escalating: continue simple moist packing (saline gauze) and regular dressing changes until it closes.
why_wrong_block:
B. Negative-pressure therapy is for large, deep or heavily exuding wounds, or slow or stalled healing (e.g. after debriding a necrotic wound); a wound already granulating well does not need it.
C. Primary closure is done at the end of the operation; a wound deliberately left open is closed later only by planned delayed primary or secondary closure. This one is healing well by secondary intention, so simple dressings continue.
D. No redness, purulence or fever means no infection; antibiotics would treat nothing.
key_concept:
Open postoperative wound: match the dressing to the wound state.
  • Clean, granulating: simple moist dressings, heal by secondary intention
  • Necrotic tissue: debride first
  • Large or exudative after debridement: VAC (negative pressure)
  • Infected (redness, pus, fever): open, drain, then antibiotics if cellulitis or systemic signs
  • Free-draining seroma without inflammation: regular dressings
exam_pearl: Healthy granulation and no infection = do not escalate; keep doing simple dressings.

stem: A 6-month-old infant presents to the Emergency Room with sudden apnea and color change. The mother gave history of recurrent vomiting, and muitiple chest infection. On examination, he looks failing to thrive with dystonic neck posturing while crying. Which of the following considers as high-risk case for the above disease?
why_right: The picture is infant GERD: "recurrent vomiting" plus "multiple chest infection" (aspiration), "failing to thrive", apnea/color change (ALTE/BRUE from reflux) and "dystonic neck posturing" (Sandifer syndrome). Preterm infants are the classic high-risk group because their lower esophageal sphincter is immature, with more transient inappropriate relaxations.
why_wrong_block:
A. Obesity is a GERD risk factor in older children and adults, not the recognized high-risk group in infancy.
C. Pertussis causes paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting and apnea, but a past pertussis infection is not a recognized risk factor for infant reflux or Sandifer syndrome.
D. Hernia repair is not linked to GERD; post-anesthesia apnea risk after hernia repair relates to prematurity itself, not reflux.
key_concept:
Infant GERD with complications: vomiting + aspiration + FTT + Sandifer posturing.
  • Sandifer syndrome = dystonic neck/back arching from reflux, mimics seizures
  • Mechanism: transient inappropriate LES relaxation
  • High-risk groups: preterm, neurologic impairment (e.g. cerebral palsy), repaired esophageal atresia/TEF, chronic lung disease
  • Red flags: apnea, aspiration pneumonia, failure to thrive
exam_pearl: Dystonic neck posturing in a vomiting infant is reflux (Sandifer), not a seizure or torticollis; prematurity is the risk factor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot marks **B; compiler's line: 'Answer: Preterm infant'.

stem: A patient presents 7 days after surgery. The surgical wound is well-approximated, has clean edges, and a pink membrane is visible in the center. The wound is also itchy. What does this indicate?
why_right: At "7 days after surgery" a "well-approximated" wound with "clean edges" and a "pink membrane" (new epithelium and granulation) is in the normal proliferative phase of healing. Itching is common as the wound heals and is not a sign of infection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Wound infection shows pain, redness, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge and fever, usually from postoperative day 4 to 5; none of these are present.
B. Abnormal healing would show gaping or dehiscence, non-healing, or excess scar (hypertrophic scar or keloid); this wound has closed edges and healthy tissue.
key_concept:
Normal healing phases.
  • Hemostasis and inflammation: first days
  • Proliferation: granulation, pink new epithelium, often itchy
  • Remodeling: scar matures over months
  • Infection signs: redness, warmth, pus, fever, pain
exam_pearl: Pink tissue plus itch with clean, closed edges is reassurance, not infection.

stem: 25 yrs old patient known case of epilepsy presented post seizure attack with flat shoulder contour and the shoulder is fixed in adduction and internal rotation What is the type of dislocation?
highlight_terms_source: fixed in adduction and internal rotation
why_right: A seizure ("known case of epilepsy... post seizure") with a "flat shoulder contour" and the arm "fixed in adduction and internal rotation" is the classic posterior shoulder dislocation. The violent internal rotator contraction during a seizure drives the humeral head backwards, and the subacromial type is the common posterior form.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta) holds the arm abducted overhead, not adducted at the side.
B. Anterior dislocations hold the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, usually after a fall on an outstretched arm.
C. Subcoracoid is the most common anterior type overall, but it also holds the arm in abduction and external rotation and is not the seizure-associated type.
key_concept:
Shoulder dislocation by arm position.
  • Anterior (most common): abducted, externally rotated, fall on outstretched arm
  • Posterior: adducted, internally rotated, seizure or electric shock
  • Posterior X-ray: light bulb sign on AP, confirm with axillary view
  • Inferior (luxatio erecta): arm fixed overhead
exam_pearl: Seizure or electric shock + adducted internally rotated arm = posterior; easy to miss on an AP film.

stem: A child enters the clinic and says "hi" to the doctor then turns to the mother and says "milk". The mother gives her a bottle of milk, and the child tries to give her doll a drink. The mother shakes her head, and the child says "no". After which the child smiles and points to her own mouth and says "mouth". When her mother wipes the doll's face, the child says "me" and begins to imitate the mother's action and gives the doll a hug. What developmental age in months is this most consistent with?
why_right: The child uses several meaningful single words ("hi", "milk", "no", "mouth", "me"), points to and names a body part, and shows pretend play (feeding and hugging the doll). A vocabulary of about 6 to 10 single words with no 2-word phrases places her at 18 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 12 months imitation and 1 to 3 words fit, but naming a body part and a 6 to 10 word vocabulary come later.
B. At 15 months a child points to body parts and has a few words, but this many single words with pretend play fits 18 months.
D. At 24 months expect 2-word phrases ("me milk") and about 50 words; this child uses single words only.
key_concept:
Language milestones set the age when words are counted.
  • 12 mo: 1 to 3 words (mama/dada specific), imitation
  • 15 mo: few words, points to a body part
  • 18 mo: 6 to 10 single words, names a body part, pretend play
  • 24 mo: 2-word phrases, ~50 words
  • 36 mo: 3-word sentences
exam_pearl: Many single words but no 2-word phrase = 18 months; the first 2-word phrase moves it to 24 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot marks *C; compiler's line: 'Answer: 18'.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with a right breast lump, which has been increasing in size over the past year. Physical examination confirmed a 10×12 cm firm, mobile mass involving the upper halve of the right breast with no palpable axillary lymph nodes (see report). Core needle biopsy: Malignant phyllodes tumour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: The core biopsy has already confirmed "malignant phyllodes tumour", so the next step in any malignant tumour is staging before treatment. Malignant phyllodes spreads by blood, most often to the lung, and does not usually spread to nodes ("no palpable axillary lymph nodes"), so contrast CT of the chest is the staging step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgery comes after staging, and a "10×12 cm" tumour is too large for wide local excision; phyllodes larger than 8 cm needs mastectomy.
B. Whole body PET is not the standard staging test for phyllodes; contrast CT is used.
D. Phyllodes is a stromal tumour that does not respond to hormonal therapy, so receptor testing does not guide management.
key_concept:
Phyllodes tumour: diagnose, stage, treat.
  • Young woman, rapidly growing, large, mobile, well-circumscribed mass
  • Diagnosis: core needle biopsy
  • Malignant: stage with contrast CT (hematogenous spread, lung)
  • Small tumour: wide local excision with at least 1 cm margin
  • Larger than 8 cm: simple mastectomy
  • Axillary dissection not routine
exam_pearl: After a malignant biopsy, stage before you cut.

stem: Young patient 4 days post exploratory laparotomy has abdominal distenstion and nausea on examination diffusely distended abdomen with sluggish bowel sounds. Despite being on maximum dose of potassium his potassium level fails to increase K level 3.1 What is the possible cause?
OptB: I can't remember any of the remaining options to save my life :')
highlight_terms_source: Despite being on maximum dose of potassium his potassium level fails to increase
why_right: Day 4 after laparotomy with distension, nausea and "sluggish bowel sounds" is postoperative ileus, and hypokalaemia (K 3.1) keeps the ileus going. The decisive clue is that K "fails to increase" despite "maximum dose of potassium": refractory hypokalaemia means coexisting hypomagnesaemia. Low magnesium increases renal potassium wasting, so potassium will not correct until magnesium is replaced.
why_wrong_block:
B. Option not recalled by the source. Plausible distractors would be ongoing GI losses or inadequate dosing, but the stem stresses maximum replacement, which points to a magnesium deficit.
C. Option not recalled by the source. Alternatives such as hyperaldosteronism or diuretic use would need a supporting history; a postoperative patient refractory to K replacement is classic hypomagnesaemia.
D. Option not recalled by the source. Mechanical obstruction or anastomotic leak would explain distension but not potassium that refuses to rise with full replacement.
key_concept:
Refractory hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia = check and replace magnesium first.
  • Postop ileus: check and correct electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca) first.
  • Low Mg increases renal K excretion, so K stays low despite supplements.
  • Low Mg also impairs PTH secretion and action, causing refractory hypocalcaemia.
  • Replace Mg, then K corrects.
exam_pearl: "Despite maximum replacement" of K or Ca is the cue for magnesium, not for more of the same ion.

stem: A 35-year-old man post total thyroidectomy for multinodular goitre presented with persistent hypocalcaemia despite adequate replacement with oral and intravenous calcium. Which of the following is the most appropriate NEXT step in management?
why_right: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia that is "persistent ... despite adequate replacement with oral and intravenous calcium" is refractory, and refractory hypocalcaemia should make you think of hypomagnesaemia. Low magnesium blocks PTH secretion and causes PTH resistance, so calcium will not correct until magnesium is repleted. The lead in is "NEXT step", so checking serum magnesium comes first.
why_wrong_block:
A. Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium and magnesium loss and would worsen the hypocalcaemia. Thiazides are used in chronic hypoparathyroidism to reduce hypercalciuria, not acutely here.
B. Recombinant PTH is reserved for chronic hypoparathyroidism not controlled by calcium and active vitamin D; a reversible cause such as low magnesium must be excluded first.
D. An IV bolus of potassium chloride is never given (risk of cardiac arrest), and potassium is not the problem in this scenario.
key_concept:
Refractory hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy = check magnesium.
  • Early postop hypocalcaemia: parathyroid injury or devascularisation.
  • Tetany or Trousseau sign: check calcium, give IV calcium gluconate.
  • Not correcting despite IV and oral calcium: check and replace Mg.
  • Persistent hypoparathyroidism long term: calcium plus active vitamin D.
exam_pearl: When an electrolyte will not correct despite full replacement, the answer is magnesium.

stem: A patient in Intensive Care Unit who is post-major surgery received 15 units of blood. The patient developed bleeding from the incision; nasogastric tube and vein puncture sites. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
highlight_terms_source: bleeding from the incision; nasogastric tube and vein puncture sites
why_right: "15 units of blood" is a massive transfusion, and stored packed cells contain no functional platelets, so the platelet count is diluted. The result is diffuse oozing from "the incision, nasogastric tube and vein puncture sites", a typical platelet/coagulopathy bleeding pattern. Dilutional thrombocytopenia is the most likely cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Citrate in stored blood can cause hypocalcaemia after massive transfusion, but it presents with perioral tingling, tetany, arrhythmia and hypotension rather than diffuse oozing; it is the answer when the question asks for the commonest metabolic complication of massive transfusion.
C. An acute haemolytic reaction gives fever, hypotension, back pain and haemoglobinuria soon after starting a unit; nothing here suggests it, while the volume transfused points to dilution.
D. Von Willebrand disease is congenital with a lifelong bleeding history; new bleeding after 15 units in ICU is acquired.
key_concept:
Massive transfusion complications:
  • Diffuse bleeding: dilutional thrombocytopenia (and dilution of clotting factors).
  • Citrate toxicity: hypocalcaemia (tingling, tetany, arrhythmia).
  • Hypothermia, hyperkalaemia, acidosis.
  • Prevention: balanced transfusion with plasma and platelets alongside red cells.
  • Bleeding plus organ failure in sepsis: think DIC instead.
exam_pearl: Bleeding question after massive transfusion = thrombocytopenia; "most likely complication" without bleeding is often hypocalcaemia.

stem: A patient notices one or more sharply marginated, scaling, and red plaques predominantly involving only the vulva. Psoriasis is suspected. Which of the following is required for a definitive diagnosis of psoriasis?
highlight_terms_source: sharply marginated, scaling, and red plaques
why_right: The lead in asks what is required for a definitive diagnosis, not how psoriasis is usually diagnosed. Histology (acanthosis, parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, neutrophil microabscesses) is the only option that confirms it. On the vulva, plaques often lose their typical scale and mimic lichen simplex, lichen sclerosus, candidiasis or VIN, so biopsy is the confirmatory test.
why_wrong_block:
B. Staining using iodine: Lugol iodine (Schiller test) is used on the cervix and vagina to outline abnormal epithelium; it does not diagnose psoriasis.
C. Clinical diagnosis is sufficient: true for typical psoriasis in everyday practice, but the question asks for a definitive diagnosis, which needs histology; right when the lead in is 'how is it usually diagnosed'.
D. Potassium hydroxide skin scraping: confirms fungal infection (hyphae or yeast) such as tinea cruris or candidiasis; useful to exclude a mimic, not to prove psoriasis.
key_concept:
'Definitive' or 'confirm' in the lead in points to histology, even for diseases usually diagnosed clinically.
  • Typical psoriasis: clinical diagnosis in practice
  • Definitive diagnosis: skin biopsy
  • KOH scraping: fungal infection
  • Lugol iodine: cervix and vagina screening aid
  • Vulvar psoriasis: often non scaly, well demarcated red plaques
exam_pearl: Read the verb: 'usually diagnosed' is clinical, 'definitive diagnosis' is biopsy.

stem: Patient presented to the clinic with eye redness on examination there is bilateral redness and wet discharge. Asking about next step in management?
OptD: Something about observe and wet wipes or eye drops ( can’t remember exactly)
key_concept:
Bilateral red eye with discharge and no red flags = conjunctivitis, usually self-limiting.
  • Watery + URTI + preauricular node: viral, supportive care
  • Purulent, lids stuck in morning: bacterial, hygiene ± topical antibiotic
  • Itch + watery + atopy: allergic, antihistamine or mast cell stabiliser drops
  • Hyperacute copious pus: gonococcal, systemic antibiotic, urgent referral
  • Red flags (pain, photophobia, reduced vision, unequal pupil): refer
exam_pearl: Topical steroid for an undiagnosed red eye is the classic wrong move.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 38-year-old patient developed a painful swelling in the right lower quadrant of his abdomen after moving a heavy object. Examination confirmed a localized tender swelling in the right lower abdominal quadrant with negative cough impulse; it persisted even with contraction of abdominal muscles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: persisted even with contraction of abdominal muscles
why_right: "After moving a heavy object" raises intra-abdominal pressure and can rupture an epigastric vessel (classically the inferior epigastric artery) inside the rectus sheath. The swelling is tender, has a "negative cough impulse" and "persisted even with contraction of abdominal muscles", which places it within the abdominal wall rather than inside the abdomen or through a defect. This is a rectus sheath haematoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. A ventral hernia usually has a positive cough impulse and is reducible; here the cough impulse is negative and the onset is acute and painful after strain.
B. An appendicular mass follows days of appendicitis with fever and leukocytosis, is not linked to lifting, and is intra-abdominal so it becomes impalpable when the wall is tensed.
C. An extraperitoneal lipoma is a slowly growing, soft, non-tender lump, not an acutely painful swelling after strain.
key_concept:
Abdominal wall mass + tensing the rectus (Fothergill sign):
  • Mass still palpable on tensing: in the wall (rectus sheath haematoma).
  • Mass disappears on tensing: intra-abdominal.
  • Positive cough impulse: hernia.
  • Precipitants: heavy lifting, coughing, anticoagulation.
  • Stable patient: conservative (rest and analgesia).
exam_pearl: Painful lump after straining with no cough impulse that stays on tensing the abdomen = rectus sheath haematoma, not a hernia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: young patient after lifting heavy object, RLQ pain and swelling persisting despite abdominal muscle contraction; options A. Ventral Hernia, B. Rectus sheath hematoma, C. Deep subfascial lipoma. Screenshot marks **D Rectus sheath hematoma.

stem: A 45-year-old is presented following poly-trauma. He requires intubation to protect airway obstruction. After resuscitation and management, he is transferred to ICU. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to clear the cervical spine?
OptD: AP and Lateral view cervical spine x-ray
why_right: The patient is "intubated" after polytrauma, so he cannot be examined or report neck pain and clinical clearance is impossible. CT of the cervical spine is the imaging of choice to clear the spine in trauma, especially in obtunded or intubated patients. It is more sensitive than plain films and fast enough for an ICU polytrauma patient.
why_wrong_block:
B. Clinical clearance (NEXUS or Canadian C-spine rules) needs an alert, sober, examinable patient without distracting injury; it is the answer only in a conscious low-risk patient.
C. MRI is for suspected ligamentous or cord injury, neurological deficit with normal CT, or persistent concern after CT; it is not the first study to clear the spine.
D. AP and lateral X-rays miss a significant proportion of injuries and are inferior to CT; they are used only where CT is unavailable.
key_concept:
Cervical spine clearance in trauma:
  • Alert, low-risk patient meeting clinical rules: clinical clearance.
  • Unconscious, intubated or high-risk: CT cervical spine.
  • Neurological deficit or suspected ligament/cord injury: MRI.
  • Keep the collar on until cleared.
exam_pearl: Intubated or obtunded = cannot clear clinically; CT is the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: MVA with suspected cervical injury, intubated, in ICU and stable; how to confirm/exclude cervical injury? A. CT scan, B. Supine and lateral x ray, C. MRI spine. Screenshot marks **A CT scan.

stem: A 65-year-old man with congestive heart failure and osteoarthritis moved into a nursing home 3 months ago. During the past 4 weeks, the patient has lost 3.6 kg, lost interest in all social activities, and has been crying almost every day. The mood is worse in the morning. At times, especially when the mood is impaired, the patient's short-term memory appears to be lost. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: lost interest in all social activities
mood is worse in the morning
when the mood is impaired, the patient's short-term memory appears to be lost
why_right: After a major life change (moving to a nursing home) he has 4 weeks of weight loss, loss of interest, daily crying and mood worse in the morning. These are features of a major depressive episode, and the memory loss that appears when the mood is low is depressive pseudodementia, which improves when the depression is treated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multi-infarct dementia: stepwise cognitive decline with focal deficits; memory loss would not wax and wane with mood.
B. Alzheimer's disease: insidious, progressive memory loss over years, with mood change appearing later; not a 4-week mood syndrome with mood-linked forgetfulness.
C. Hypothyroidism: can cause low mood and slowing, but typically with weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation; here he is losing weight.
key_concept:
Pseudodementia (depression) vs dementia:
  • Depression: subacute onset, mood symptoms first, memory fluctuates with mood, "I don't know" answers
  • Dementia: insidious onset, memory first, patient minimizes deficits
  • Diurnal variation (worse in morning) favors depression
exam_pearl: Memory loss that worsens with low mood in an elderly person after a life change is depression, not dementia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version options: A. Alzheimer's disease, B. Depression, C. Multiple infarction dementia (memory loss fluctuates with mood). Answer: D refers to the Q: version (Depression).

stem: Child 9 yrs has bed wetting and mother mentioned that he was dry since the age of six years. His mother noticed foul smelling urine and change in urine color. There is positive nitrite and leukocytes. Culture: gram negative bacilli bacteria. WBCs > 100,000. What is the most common organism causing this condition?
highlight_terms_source: dry since the age of six years
why_right: Secondary enuresis ("dry since the age of six"), foul smelling discolored urine, positive nitrite and leukocytes and a Gram negative bacillus at >100,000 CFU/ml confirm a UTI. E. coli is by far the most common cause of pediatric UTI (roughly 80 to 90 percent).
why_wrong_block:
B. Proteus is a urease producer (alkaline urine, struvite stones), more typical in uncircumcised boys or stone disease; it is a less common cause than E. coli.
C. Klebsiella is a Gram negative cause of UTI but much less common, seen more in hospital acquired or complicated infections.
D. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram positive coccus causing pneumonia, otitis and meningitis, not a urinary pathogen with Gram negative bacilli.
key_concept:
New bedwetting after being dry = secondary enuresis; rule out UTI, diabetes, stress.
  • Most common UTI organism: E. coli
  • Nitrite positive = Gram negative (nitrate reducing) bacteria
  • Significant bacteriuria on clean catch: >100,000 CFU/ml of one organism
  • Proteus: alkaline urine, struvite stones
exam_pearl: Secondary enuresis is a symptom, not a diagnosis; dipstick nitrite + leukocytes points to UTI, and the bug is E. coli.

stem: 25 years old man presented to the clinic and he seems to be looking frequently at the corner of the room when asked he said “my mother is standing there, but others can’t see her only me”. When relatives from his family were asked they said that his mother died when he was 5 years old. What does he have or what is the cause of this?
highlight_terms_source: my mother is standing there, but others can’t see her only me
why_right: He sees his mother standing in the corner when no one else can, and she died years ago. A perception without an external stimulus is a hallucination, and since the modality is sight (he keeps looking at the corner), it is a visual hallucination.
why_wrong_block:
B. Auditory hallucinations: hearing voices without a stimulus; he describes seeing her, not hearing her.
C. Episode of disorganized thoughts: a disorder of thought form (derailment, loose associations, incoherent speech); his answer is clear and goal directed.
D. Delusion: a fixed false belief (a thought problem), not a sensory perception; it would be a delusion if he believed she was alive without perceiving her.
key_concept:
Perception vs belief vs thought form:
  • Hallucination: perception without stimulus (visual, auditory, tactile...)
  • Illusion: misinterpretation of a real stimulus
  • Delusion: fixed false belief
  • Disorganized thinking: abnormal thought form
exam_pearl: "I see her but others can't" is a perception, so hallucination; name the modality from the sense used.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version (screenshot on next page): 27-year-old kept looking to the right, 'My mother is there, but no one can see her except me', she comes and goes, family says she died when he was a child; options A. Delusion, **B. Visual hallucination, C. Auditory hallucination, D. Episode of disorganized thinking. Same answer (visual hallucination).

stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the clinic with history of hearing voices coming from the toaster and refrigerator, warning that all the food is poisoned. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: He hears voices coming from the toaster and refrigerator. Hearing voices with no real speaker is a perception without a stimulus in the auditory modality, so the core phenomenon is an auditory hallucination, the most common type in psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Delusional thinking: a fixed false belief. Believing the food is poisoned could be a secondary delusion, but the question describes the voices themselves, which are a perceptual disturbance.
B. Visual hallucination: would require seeing things that are not there; he hears, not sees.
C. Disorganized thinking: loose associations or incoherent speech; nothing about his thought form is described.
key_concept:
Classify the psychotic symptom by what is abnormal:
  • A sense (heard, seen, felt): hallucination of that modality
  • A belief (poisoned, followed): delusion
  • The flow of thought: disorganization
  • Auditory is the commonest hallucination in schizophrenia; visual suggests organic causes
exam_pearl: Voices from objects = auditory hallucination; the poisoning content tempts you to pick delusion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot only; **D marked (the word 'Delusional' in option A has a blue selection highlight, not the answer mark).

stem: Patient in ICU has sacral ulcer. The ulcer has necrotic tissue and fat clumps i think. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: An ICU patient with a sacral pressure ulcer containing "necrotic tissue" and fat needs the necrotic tissue removed first, so debridement is mandatory. A sacral pressure ulcer in a bedbound ICU patient is a chronic wound at high risk of non-healing and contamination, so after debridement it is managed with vacuum-assisted closure (negative pressure wound therapy) to remove exudate and promote granulation.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV antibiotics alone do not penetrate necrotic tissue; they are added for cellulitis, sepsis or osteomyelitis, but never replace debridement.
B. Primary closure of a contaminated, necrotic pressure wound under tension in an immobile patient will break down; closure suits a clean, fresh wound.
C. A graft will not take on a necrotic or exudative bed; grafting is done later once healthy granulation tissue is present.
key_concept:
Necrotic pressure ulcer management:
  • Necrotic tissue: debride.
  • Chronic, exudative or high-risk wound after debridement: VAC.
  • Healthy granulation bed: delayed graft or flap.
  • Always: offloading, repositioning, nutrition.
  • Antibiotics only for spreading infection, sepsis or osteomyelitis.
exam_pearl: Necrosis = debridement first; sacral pressure wound after debridement = VAC, not closure or graft.

stem: A 75-year-old man in the Intensive Care Unit has developed a discharging sacral wound. Examination confirms necrotic skin and subcutaneous fat. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A "75-year-old" ICU patient with a "discharging sacral wound" and "necrotic skin and subcutaneous fat" has an infected pressure ulcer at high risk of non-healing. Necrotic tissue must be debrided, and the resulting cavity is best managed by vacuum-assisted closure, which removes exudate, reduces oedema and promotes granulation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Primary repair without debridement leaves necrotic tissue in the wound and will fail; it suits only a clean, fresh wound.
B. Primary closure of a discharging, contaminated pressure wound will break down; debridement must be followed by open management first.
C. A primary skin graft will not take on an exudative, poorly vascularised bed; grafting comes later once granulation tissue forms.
key_concept:
Necrotic or discharging chronic wound: debride, then VAC.
  • Clean sharp wound with divided structures: primary repair.
  • Degloving or contaminated trauma: debridement and secondary grafting.
  • Sacral pressure ulcer with necrosis: debridement and VAC.
  • Graft only on a healthy granulating bed.
exam_pearl: "Discharging" and "necrotic" rule out any primary closure or primary graft.

stem: 6 months boy delivered full term vaginally without complications. Come to assess by doctor and he found him has normal development. Which of the following of gross motor development present in the infant at this age
why_right: This recall's key is sit without support because many milestone tables list sitting (initially tripod, with hand support) as the 6-month gross motor skill of a normal term infant. It is the option that defines the age, as opposed to an earlier skill already achieved.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rolling prone to supine appears around 4 months, so it is present at 6 months but is an earlier milestone, not the one that characterizes this age.
C. Mature (pincer) grasp is a fine motor skill appearing around 9 to 12 months; at 6 months the grasp is a palmar (raking) grasp.
key_concept:
Gross motor ladder in infancy.
  • 4 mo: rolls prone to supine, head steady
  • 5 to 6 mo: rolls supine to prone (both ways)
  • 6 mo: sits with tripod support; fully independent sitting about 7 to 9 mo
  • 9 mo: pulls to stand, stands holding support, pincer grasp starts
  • 12 mo: walks
exam_pearl: "Rolls supine to prone" and "tripod sitting" are both 6-month answers; prone to supine is 4 months, pincer grasp is 9 months and fine motor.

stem: Pt post MVA BP 90/60 no bleeding what is the next step:
why_right: A trauma patient after an MVA with "BP 90/60" is hypotensive, and following the ABC sequence, circulation is restored before any imaging. "No bleeding" means no visible external bleeding; hypotension in trauma is still assumed to be haemorrhage (internal) until proven otherwise. The next step is IV access and fluid resuscitation (moving to blood if there is no response), then searching for the source.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT abdomen is for the haemodynamically stable trauma patient; an unstable patient should not go to the scanner and instead gets resuscitation and FAST.
B. Brain MRI has no role in acute trauma resuscitation; head injury is imaged with CT once the patient is stabilised.
C. Observation is unsafe in a hypotensive trauma patient; it suits a stable patient with a normal assessment.
key_concept:
Trauma: ABC before imaging.
  • Circulation: two large bore IV lines, fluids, then blood if no response.
  • Control external bleeding with direct pressure; pelvic binder for pelvic bleeding.
  • Stable abdominal trauma: CT abdomen.
  • Unstable blunt abdominal trauma: FAST.
  • Unstable with positive FAST: laparotomy.
exam_pearl: Hypotension in trauma means resuscitate first; "no bleeding" does not exclude internal bleeding.

stem: Middle age man known case of chronic liver and ascites, he presented to the ER with large umbilical swelling, upon examination there was large reducible and uncomfortable umbilical hernia, abdominal distention with thinning of the skin and dilated veins. He was planned for elective hernia repair. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: In a cirrhotic patient with uncontrolled ascites, umbilical hernia repair carries a high risk of recurrence, wound leak, infection and decompensation. The hernia here is "reducible" and repair was "planned elective", so there is no emergency; the correct sequence is to control the ascites first (diuretics, sodium restriction, paracentesis or TIPS if refractory) and optimise liver function, then repair.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate repair (however the closure is reinforced) with uncontrolled ascites risks ascitic leak, wound breakdown and recurrence; immediate surgery is right only for a strangulated, incarcerated or ruptured hernia.
B. Laparoscopic mesh repair is not the priority while ascites is uncontrolled; mesh in a patient with ascites carries risk of leak and infection, and the timing problem remains.
D. A single paracentesis followed directly by open repair does not control the ascites, which reaccumulates quickly and leaks through the wound; repair should follow sustained ascites control.
key_concept:
Umbilical hernia in cirrhosis with ascites:
  • Elective, reducible: control ascites and optimise first, then repair.
  • Refractory ascites: consider TIPS before repair.
  • Strangulation, incarceration or rupture (skin ulceration, leak): emergency repair.
  • Thinned skin is a warning of rupture, so optimise without undue delay.
exam_pearl: Elective hernia plus uncontrolled ascites = fix the ascites first; complicated hernia = operate now.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: cirrhosis with ascites, reducible uncomfortable umbilical hernia planned for repair; options A. do the operation immediately, B. do not do operation, C. delay until the ascites control; Answer: C. Q: version also Answer: C.

stem: Child came complaining of generalised edema and fatigue, he had history of bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 weeks ago. Lab: Retics 3, Hb 9 or 8, Plt 55, Wbc 8, Cr high. What test would lead to diagnosis?
why_right: "Bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain 2 weeks ago" followed by edema, anemia (Hb 8 to 9 with reticulocytosis), thrombocytopenia (Plt 55) and high creatinine is post-diarrheal (typical) HUS. The test that establishes the cause is a stool study: culture for Shiga toxin producing E. coli (O157:H7) and Shiga toxin detection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood tests (smear for schistocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, Coombs) confirm microangiopathic hemolysis and are part of the workup, but they do not identify the triggering infection.
B. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria reflecting the renal injury, but it is nonspecific and does not establish the etiology.
key_concept:
HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury.
  • Typical: about 1 to 2 weeks after bloody diarrhea, STEC O157:H7 (also Shigella)
  • Etiology: stool culture / Shiga toxin
  • Smear: schistocytes; Coombs negative; normal PT/APTT (vs DIC)
  • Management: supportive (fluids, dialysis if needed); avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs
exam_pearl: Normal coagulation separates HUS from DIC; the history of bloody diarrhea sends you to the stool.

stem: Child came complaining reduced oral intake, expiratory wheeze, nasal discharge, and mild distress, no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A child with "nasal discharge" (URTI prodrome), "expiratory wheeze", "reduced oral intake" and "mild distress" with "no fever" fits viral bronchiolitis (most often RSV) in an infant. Diffuse expiratory wheeze reflects small airway obstruction and air trapping.
why_wrong_block: A. Pneumonia usually presents with fever, tachypnea and focal crackles or bronchial breathing; diffuse wheeze without fever points away from it.
key_concept:
Bronchiolitis: first wheezing episode with coryza in a child under 2 (peak under 1 year).
  • Cause: RSV most common
  • Signs: coryza, cough, wheeze and/or fine crackles, poor feeding, retractions
  • Fever often low grade or absent
  • Diagnosis is clinical; management supportive (O2 if low SpO2, hydration, suction)
  • Recurrent wheeze in an older child: think asthma
exam_pearl: Wheeze plus coryza in an infant without high fever is bronchiolitis; focal signs with high fever is pneumonia.

stem: A 34-year-old male presents to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He is found to have a pelvic fracture described as an "open-book" injury. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus and a high-riding prostate on digital rectal exam. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Blood at the urethral meatus plus a high-riding prostate after an open-book pelvic fracture means a posterior (membranous) urethral injury until proven otherwise. The lead-in asks for the next step, so the urethra must be imaged before anything is passed through it: a retrograde urethrogram confirms or excludes the tear. If it confirms injury, the bladder is then drained with a suprapubic catheter.
why_wrong_block:
A. Insert a Foley catheter: contraindicated when urethral injury is suspected, because blind passage can convert a partial tear into a complete one. Right only after a normal retrograde urethrogram.
B. Obtain a KUB CT: CT assesses kidneys, bladder and pelvic organs but does not reliably show the urethra. A CT cystogram is used for suspected bladder injury once the urethra is cleared.
D. Proceed to exploratory laparotomy: indicated for an unstable patient with positive FAST, peritonitis or evisceration. Nothing here points to an intraperitoneal injury needing surgery.
key_concept:
Blood at meatus after pelvic fracture: image the urethra before any catheter.
  • Clues: blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, inability to void, perineal/scrotal hematoma
  • Most vulnerable segment in pelvic fracture: membranous (posterior) urethra
  • Step 1: retrograde urethrogram
  • Injury confirmed: suprapubic catheter (cystostomy)
  • Urethrogram normal: Foley is then allowed
exam_pearl: If the question says the urethrogram already shows disruption, the answer moves on to suprapubic catheter, never Foley.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's first version: 'Patient post MVA vitally stable, blood in meatus, open book frature with bilatral pubic rami, next step? A. CT nephron pyelogram B. Retrograde urethrogram C. supra pubic catheter' (no answer marked). Other versions: 25 yo motorcycle accident, unstable pelvic fracture, blood at meatus, initial imaging? (A CT with contrast, B Retrograde urethrogram, C Pelvic angiography, D Pelvic MRI) Answer: B. Retrograde urethrogram; 24 yo MVA, blood at meatus, can't void, high riding prostate, best to diagnose? (A IV pyelogram, B Insert Foley's, C CT cystogram, D Retrograde urethrogram) Answer: D. Retrograde urethrogram.

stem: Child came with increasing vague abdominal pain and bruises in abdomen has history of falling from bicycle days ago what is next step?
why_right: A child with increasing abdominal pain and abdominal wall bruising after a bicycle fall (classic handlebar mechanism) may have a delayed solid organ, pancreatic or duodenal injury. With no sign of instability, the rule for hemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma applies: CT abdomen with IV contrast is the investigation that defines these injuries.
why_wrong_block:
B. US abdomen: FAST looks for free fluid and is the tool for the unstable patient; it misses pancreatic, duodenal and hollow viscus injuries, which are exactly what a handlebar blow causes.
C. Reassure: worsening pain with abdominal wall bruising days after trauma is a red flag for a missed internal injury, so discharge without imaging is unsafe. Right only for a well child with a normal exam and no bruising.
key_concept:
Blunt abdominal trauma: stability decides the test.
  • Stable: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Unstable blunt: FAST
  • Unstable + FAST positive: laparotomy
  • Handlebar bruise: think duodenal hematoma, pancreatic injury, bowel injury
exam_pearl: Abdominal wall bruising (seat belt or handlebar sign) is a reason to image, not to reassure.

stem: Women ( i think post partum lactating) complains of breast tenderness and erythema with mass measuring appx. 2 × 3 cm on exam US done and showed mass measuring 3×4 cm filled with thick fluids, DDx are breast abscess, complicated cycts and another differential I forgot, for clinical correlation. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A lactating woman with a tender red breast and an ultrasound showing a thick fluid-filled collection has a breast abscess, not simple mastitis. The collection is 3 × 4 cm (under 5 cm), single, and no thinned or necrotic skin is described, so first-line treatment is needle (ultrasound-guided) aspiration, given together with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics and repeated if it reaccumulates. Aspiration also sends fluid for culture and helps exclude a complicated cyst.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone: enough for mastitis without a collection (no fluctuation). Once pus is seen on ultrasound it must be drained; antibiotics are an adjunct.
C. Incision and drainage: reserved for an abscess of about 5 cm or larger, multiple abscesses, thinned, ischemic or necrotic overlying skin, or failure of repeated aspiration.
key_concept:
Lactational breast infection ladder:
  • Tender red breast, no collection: mastitis, anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (flucloxacillin), keep breastfeeding
  • Fluctuant mass or collection on US: abscess
  • Abscess under 5 cm, single, healthy skin: needle aspiration + antibiotics
  • About 5 cm or more, multiple, thinned/necrotic skin: incision and drainage
exam_pearl: Look for the size and the skin: thinned or necrotic skin flips aspiration to incision and drainage.

stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with abdominal pain for 5 days and yellowish discoloration of the sclera, associated with fever and chills. Laboratory results: WBC: 19 × 10⁹/L; Indirect bilirubin: 7; Direct bilirubin: 18; Total bilirubin: 25; Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): 250. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Abdominal pain, yellow sclera and fever with chills complete Charcot's triad. The labs show infection (WBC 19) plus obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice: bilirubin mainly direct (18 of 25) and raised ALP 250. Infection on top of bile duct obstruction is ascending cholangitis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Acute cholecystitis: fever, prolonged RUQ pain and Murphy sign, but bilirubin is usually normal or only mildly raised because the common bile duct is patent. Marked conjugated jaundice points to the duct.
C. Biliary colic: transient postprandial pain with no fever, no leukocytosis and normal liver tests. Five days of pain with fever excludes it.
D. Hepatic (gallbladder) mucocele: cystic duct obstruction with a distended, often non-tender palpable gallbladder filled with mucus; it does not cause fever with leukocytosis and conjugated jaundice.
key_concept:
RUQ pain spectrum: add one feature at a time.
  • Biliary colic: pain only, normal labs
  • Acute cholecystitis: pain + fever + leukocytosis, Murphy sign, bilirubin near normal
  • Choledocholithiasis: pain + obstructive jaundice, no fever
  • Cholangitis: Charcot triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice)
  • Reynolds pentad: + hypotension + confusion
exam_pearl: Jaundice with fever is cholangitis; jaundice without fever is choledocholithiasis.

stem: Pediatric with seizure and Fatigue other signs, Hepatomegaly and Cataract Blood Culture: E.coli labs showed metabolic acidosis urine analysis: aminoaciduria and glycosuria What's the diagnosis?
why_right: "Hepatomegaly", "cataract" and E. coli sepsis are the classic triad clue for galactosemia (GALT deficiency). Accumulated galactose-1-phosphate damages the liver and renal tubules (Fanconi picture: "aminoaciduria and glycosuria" with metabolic acidosis), galactitol causes cataract, and hypoglycemia can cause seizures.
why_wrong_block:
B. Homocystinuria causes lens dislocation (downward), marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability and thrombosis, not cataract with liver failure and E. coli sepsis.
C. Methylmalonic acidemia causes severe anion gap metabolic acidosis with ketosis and hyperammonemia, but not cataract, Fanconi syndrome or E. coli sepsis.
D. Maple syrup urine disease presents with poor feeding, encephalopathy and burnt sugar smelling urine; it lacks cataract and hepatomegaly.
key_concept:
Galactosemia (classic, GALT deficiency, autosomal recessive).
  • Onset after milk feeding: vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive
  • Cataract (galactitol), renal Fanconi (aminoaciduria, glycosuria, acidosis)
  • E. coli neonatal sepsis is a hallmark
  • Urine reducing substances positive
  • Treatment: remove galactose/lactose (soy based formula)
exam_pearl: Cataract + liver disease + E. coli sepsis = galactosemia; lens dislocation instead points to homocystinuria.

stem: Cough , fevere developed SOB , on examination the child looks well basal crackles on rt lower chest auscaltation , stony dullness on percussion , T 38.5 ?
key_concept:
Percussion decides the chest finding.
  • Stony dullness = pleural effusion
  • Dull + bronchial breathing = consolidation (pneumonia)
  • Hyperresonant + absent breath sounds = pneumothorax
  • Dull + trachea shifted toward the side = collapse
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to pleural effusion.
exam_pearl: Stony dullness means fluid in the pleural space; plain dullness with bronchial breathing means consolidation.

stem: Perforated diverticulitis + abscess collection 6.8 cm , vitally stable ( vitals provided no hypotension nor fever) ?
why_right: This is complicated diverticulitis with a contained abscess (Hinchey II) rather than free perforation with peritonitis. The patient is vitally stable and the abscess is large (6.8 cm), too big to resolve on antibiotics alone, so the standard is image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics, avoiding emergency surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotic alone: right for uncomplicated diverticulitis or a small abscess (roughly under 3 to 4 cm). A 6.8 cm collection needs drainage.
B. Exploration: right for purulent or feculent peritonitis (Hinchey III/IV), hemodynamic instability, or failure of percutaneous drainage. None of these is present.
key_concept:
Hinchey decides management of complicated diverticulitis:
  • I (small pericolic abscess): antibiotics
  • II (larger pelvic or distant abscess): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • III (purulent peritonitis) / IV (feculent peritonitis): surgery
  • Diagnosis: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Colonoscopy 6 to 8 weeks later to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: The word "perforated" alone does not mean laparotomy: stable with a contained abscess means drain; generalized peritonitis or instability means operate.

stem: Man old age left lower abdominal pain , constipation, vitals normal except fever 38.5 WBCs 18 initial next step?
key_concept:
Suspected acute diverticulitis (LLQ pain, fever, leukocytosis):
  • Investigation of choice: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Treat: antibiotics (bowel rest if more unwell), drainage for a large abscess
  • Never scope in the acute phase
  • Colonoscopy after 6 to 8 weeks
exam_pearl: Fork: an acute inflammatory picture (fever, leukocytosis) points to treating the attack; colonoscopy belongs to the quiet phase 6 to 8 weeks later.

stem: Old man known case of diverticulosis, came complaining of mild intermittent left lower abdominal pain, has no fever normal WBCs and no signs of peritonitis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: mild intermittent left lower abdominal pain
no fever normal WBCs and no signs of peritonitis
key_concept:
Diverticular disease ladder:
  • Diverticulosis / mild intermittent pain, normal WBC, afebrile: high fiber and fluids
  • Suspected diverticulitis (fever, WBC up, tenderness): CT with contrast, then antibiotics
  • Large abscess: percutaneous drainage
  • Generalized peritonitis: surgery
exam_pearl: The listed negatives are the fork: fever, raised WBC or peritonitis push toward CT, antibiotics or surgery; their absence points to conservative dietary care.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Examiner: All these negatives were literally stated in the question (no fever, normal WBC, no signs of peritonitis).

stem: Child with head trauma vomited then came to ED drowsy and dilated pupil , CT small epidural hematoma no midline shift ?
why_right: An epidural hematoma is treated by the patient's neurology, not only by its size on CT. This child is drowsy with a dilated pupil after vomiting, meaning deteriorating consciousness and early uncal herniation. Any EDH with neurological deterioration or a pupillary abnormality needs urgent surgical evacuation, even if "small" and without midline shift, because arterial bleeding can expand quickly.
why_wrong_block:
B. Repeat CT: suitable for a small EDH in a fully alert child with no focal deficit, managed with close neuro observation. A dilated pupil removes the option of waiting.
C. Mannitol: a temporizing measure to lower intracranial pressure while theatre is arranged; it does not treat the bleed and is not the definitive answer.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma:
  • Source: middle meningeal artery, often with temporal fracture
  • CT: biconvex (lens shaped) collection
  • Classic: lucid interval then rapid decline
  • Surgery: large hematoma, midline shift, falling GCS, or pupil asymmetry / focal deficit
  • Non-operative only if small AND neurologically intact, with repeat CT
exam_pearl: A blown pupil makes a "small" epidural surgical; treat the patient, not the scan.

stem: Girl presented with bleeding per rectum , watery diarrhea , long standing nausea , epigastric pain?
key_concept:
Alarm features in pediatric GI complaints require investigation.
  • GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss / growth failure, nocturnal symptoms, persistent vomiting
  • Bloody diarrhea: infectious colitis, IBD
  • Painless large rectal bleed: Meckel (technetium scan)
  • Empirical PPI only for dyspepsia without alarm features
exam_pearl: Alarm features (bleeding, anemia, weight loss, growth failure) decide between investigating and treating empirically or reassuring.
